question: Why doesn't passive immunity give long-term protection?

options.A: The recipient's immune cells fail to develop memory cells
options.B: Pathogens mutate too quickly for transferred antibodies to bind
options.C: White blood cells actively destroy all foreign immunoglobulins
options.D: The liver metabolizes the antibodies into inactive amino acids

explanation: Because the body is never exposed to the antigen to trigger its own response, no memory cells are created. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h1)

question: Which antibody crosses the human placenta to protect the foetus?
explanation: IgG is the only antibody type that can cross the placental barrier to provide passive immunity to the unborn baby. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h2)

question: Why is a baby born prematurely at 28 weeks at a higher risk of infection?

options.A: Breast milk completely lacks antibodies during the first month of life
options.B: Premature infants produce their own active white blood cells too quickly
options.C: They missed the critical period of transplacental IgG transfer in late pregnancy
options.D: Their mucosal membranes cannot secrete any form of protective IgA

explanation: Most maternal IgG transfer happens during the third trimester, so early preterm babies are born with very low antibody stores. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h2)

question: When is artificial passive immunity usually given to a patient?

options.A: Years before planned travel to build lifelong immune memory
options.B: When immediate protection is needed after a high-risk exposure
options.C: Once a chronic infection has fully established itself in tissues
options.D: As a routine replacement for standard childhood vaccines

explanation: Artificial passive immunity provides instant antibodies for urgent situations where waiting for active immunization is unsafe. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h3)

question: What is the main difference between artificial passive immunity and active vaccination?

options.A: Passive immunity supplies ready-made antibodies instead of stimulating the body to make them
options.B: Vaccines protect only temporarily whereas passive therapy lasts a lifetime
options.C: Vaccines provide instantaneous protection while passive products take weeks to work
options.D: Passive immunity relies on live weakened viruses rather than killed bacteria

explanation: Active vaccines force the immune system to build its own defense, while passive immunity hands over external antibodies. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h3)

question: How quickly does passive immunity begin protecting the body after administration?
explanation: Because the antibodies are already fully formed, they start neutralizing target agents right away without any delay. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h4)

question: What happens to passive antibodies in the human body over time?

options.A: They are gradually broken down and cleared from circulation
options.B: They bind permanently to host tissues and remain there forever
options.C: They transform into active memory cells to fight future infections
options.D: They multiply inside the bone marrow to form a permanent reserve

explanation: The body treats introduced antibodies like any other circulating protein, breaking them down over several weeks or months. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h4)

question: A woman with a rhesus-negative blood type gives birth to a rhesus-positive baby in a clinic. What is the best action?

options.A: Give the newborn a live polio vaccine immediately to stimulate active immunity
options.B: Schedule the mother for routine tetanus toxoid booster injections next week
options.C: Provide oral broad-spectrum antibiotics to clear maternal white blood cells
options.D: Administer anti-D immunoglobulin to prevent maternal antibody sensitization

explanation: Anti-D immunoglobulin clears any fetal cells that entered the mother's blood, stopping her immune system from forming antibodies against future rhesus-positive babies. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a standard use of passive immunisation?

options.A: Stopping rhesus incompatibility reactions in pregnant women
options.B: Preventing disease after a deep puncture wound contaminated with soil
options.C: Providing immediate antibody cover following a rabid animal bite
options.D: Building lifelong immunity through routine childhood measles vaccination

explanation: Vaccines stimulate active immunity and long-term memory, which is different from passive immunization. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h5)

question: Why can someone who received passive antibodies for tetanus still catch tetanus months later?

options.A: The body formed no memory cells to recognize the bacteria in the future
options.B: The original antibodies mutated into harmful antigens over time
options.C: Live bacteria destroyed all the circulating white blood cells
options.D: The initial dose permanently suppressed the patient's bone marrow

explanation: Passive immunity bypasses the body's immune learning process, leaving no memory cells to protect against later infections. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h6)

question: What is a known complication of using animal-derived antisera?

options.A: Excessive production of endogenous red blood cells
options.B: Permanent transformation of recipient blood type
options.D: Immediate lifelong immunity to multiple viruses

explanation: Foreign proteins from animal sera can cause allergic or adverse immune reactions in humans, such as serum sickness. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T8#BMP111_U6_T8_h6)

question: What is the main difference between natural immunity and artificial immunity?

options.A: It requires synthetic vaccines to be effective
options.B: It relies entirely on pharmaceutical treatments
options.C: It develops without medical intervention or immunization
options.D: It only functions during the first week of life

explanation: Natural immunity happens through normal daily life exposures and natural body processes rather than through vaccines or medical treatments. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h1)

question: How does innate natural immunity compare to adaptive natural immunity?

options.A: Adaptive immunity is present fully formed before birth
options.B: Innate immunity requires previous exposure to a specific pathogen
options.C: Adaptive immunity offers no immunological memory for future infections
options.D: Innate immunity provides immediate, non-specific protection from birth

explanation: The innate system acts as the body's first line of defense, reacting to all germs in a general way without needing prior exposure. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h1)

question: Which cells create long-term memory in the immune system after a natural infection?
explanation: Memory cells stay in the body long after an infection clears, ready to recognize and fight off the same germ if it returns. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h2)

question: Why is active natural immunity called 'active'?

options.A: The body actively manufactures its own antibodies and immune cells
options.B: It involves receiving ready-made antibodies from another person
options.C: It requires physical activity and exercise to function properly
options.D: It only works when the heart pumps at a faster rate

explanation: Active immunity means the person's own body does the work of fighting the infection and producing protective cells and antibodies. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h2)

question: Which antibody class passes from the mother to the baby across the placenta during pregnancy?
explanation: IgG is the specific antibody type that can cross the human placenta to provide passive protection to the developing fetus. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h3)

question: A mother asks why exclusive breastfeeding helps protect her young baby from stomach bugs. What is the reason?

options.A: Breast milk kills all bacteria permanently so infections can never happen
options.B: Breast milk delivers maternal IgA antibodies directly to line the baby's gut
options.C: Breast milk replaces the need for any future childhood vaccinations
options.D: Breast milk forces the baby's bone marrow to create permanent memory cells

explanation: Secretory IgA in breast milk coats the infant's digestive tract, helping neutralize local germs safely. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h3)

question: What is the main job of antigen-presenting cells in natural immunity?

options.A: Pumping blood and oxygen throughout the lymphatic system
options.B: Engulfing pathogens and displaying their fragments to other immune cells
options.C: Producing red blood cells inside the bone marrow
options.D: Creating physical barriers like skin and mucous membranes

explanation: These cells capture invaders and show pieces of them to T-cells and B-cells to trigger a targeted defense. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h4)

question: What is the function of cytokines during an immune response?

options.A: They act as chemical messengers to stimulate other immune cells
options.B: They form a hard physical wall around the infected tissue
options.C: They transport oxygen molecules directly to lymphocytes
options.D: They dissolve the cell walls of beneficial bacteria

explanation: Cytokines are signaling proteins released by immune cells to coordinate the attack and manage the body's response. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h4)

question: Why can high levels of maternal antibodies in a newborn interfere with some early childhood vaccines?

options.A: The maternal antibodies may neutralize the vaccine antigens before the infant's immune system responds
options.B: The maternal antibodies cause permanent damage to the infant's bone marrow
options.C: The vaccine will cause the mother's own immune system to react violently
options.D: The infant's body will immediately excrete all vaccines through the digestive tract

explanation: Remaining maternal antibodies can attach to vaccine particles just like real germs, which stops the infant's own immune system from building a response. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a safe way to build lasting immunity against dangerous childhood diseases?

options.B: Allowing the infant to consume nutrient-rich colostrum
options.C: Deliberately exposing a child to wild natural infections
options.D: Receiving protective antibodies via transplacental transfer

explanation: Intentionally exposing children to natural infections is unsafe because it risks severe complications and illness compared to standard immunizations. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T9#BMP111_U6_T9_h5)

question: What is the main waste gas that the respiratory system removes from the body?
explanation: Cellular activity produces carbon dioxide as a waste product, and the lungs clear it from the bloodstream. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why is knowing how breathing works important for midwives?

options.A: Midwives only treat lung diseases and never handle normal deliveries.
options.B: Fetal lungs do not develop until the mother stops breathing room air.
options.C: The respiratory system shuts down completely during the second trimester.
options.D: Pregnancy changes how a woman breathes and raises her need for oxygen.

explanation: The body's changing demands mean midwives need to keep an eye on breathing health throughout pregnancy. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which structure marks the dividing line between the upper and lower respiratory tracts?
explanation: The larynx is the transition point where the upper airway meets the lower breathing structures in the chest. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h2)

question: A pregnant patient has an infection limited to her nose and throat. Which part of her respiratory system is affected?
explanation: The nose and pharynx are key parts of the upper respiratory tract, located outside the chest cavity. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is the main job of the blood vessels inside the nasal cavity?
explanation: Blood vessels in the nose warm up the air as it enters, protecting the delicate tissues of the lower lungs. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a function of the upper respiratory tract?

options.D: Direct exchange of oxygen with blood cells

explanation: Gas exchange happens only in the tiny air sacs of the lower lungs, not in the upper airways. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h3)

question: What stops the windpipe from collapsing when a person breathes in?
explanation: Stiff rings of cartilage provide support to keep the windpipe open at all times. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h4)

question: Where does the actual exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide happen in the lungs?
explanation: Alveoli are tiny, thin-walled sacs next to blood vessels that allow gases to move quickly back and forth. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which hormone helps stimulate breathing changes during pregnancy?
explanation: Higher levels of progesterone affect the brainstem, causing women to breathe a bit deeper and faster. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h5)

question: How does the growing uterus affect the diaphragm in late pregnancy?

options.A: It pulls the diaphragm downward toward the pelvic floor.
options.B: It pushes the diaphragm upward into the chest cavity.
options.C: It paralyzes the muscle fibers of the diaphragm completely.
options.D: It wraps around the diaphragm to restrict all chest movement.

explanation: As the baby grows, the uterus pushes upward, changing the shape and space inside the chest. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T1#BMP121_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of pulmonary ventilation in the human body?

options.A: Pumping oxygen-rich blood to the brain
options.B: Moving air in and out of the lungs
options.C: Creating sound vibrations for human speech
options.D: Filtering dust particles from the nasal cavity

explanation: Pulmonary ventilation refers specifically to the mechanical movement of air into and out of the respiratory tract. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why does air naturally flow into the lungs during a normal breath?

options.A: The heart acts as a secondary pump for air movement
options.B: Active muscular contraction directly squeezes the lung tissue
options.C: A pressure difference exists between the atmosphere and alveoli
options.D: Surface tension pulls ambient air through the trachea

explanation: Air always moves down its pressure gradient, flowing from a region of higher pressure to a lower pressure area inside the chest. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which muscle forms the primary floor of the thoracic cavity and drives quiet breathing?
explanation: The diaphragm is the main dome-shaped muscle responsible for the majority of normal, quiet breathing work. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h2)

question: Where are the intercostal muscles located in the human body?
explanation: Intercostal muscles sit directly between adjacent ribs, helping to elevate or depress the rib cage during respiration. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h2)

question: How do pressure and volume relate to each other according to Boyle's law?

options.A: They remain completely constant during breathing
options.B: They have a direct positive relationship
options.D: They increase together at the same rate

explanation: When the volume of a container goes up, the gas pressure inside it goes down, which is the core principle of Boyle's law. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h3)

question: What happens to the pressure inside the lungs when the chest cavity expands in volume?

options.A: Lung pressure drops briefly to absolute zero
options.B: Lung pressure stays exactly equal to the outside air
options.C: Lung pressure increases above atmospheric pressure
options.D: Lung pressure decreases below atmospheric pressure

explanation: Expanding the chest increases volume, which lowers the pressure inside, causing outside air to rush in. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which phase of normal, quiet breathing requires active muscular contraction?
explanation: Inhalation requires the active contraction of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, whereas quiet exhalation relies on passive recoil. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why does quiet expiration happen without much muscular effort?

options.A: Elastic lung tissues recoil and the diaphragm relaxes
options.B: Atmospheric pressure actively compresses the trachea
options.C: Abdominal muscles push all remaining air outward
options.D: Gravity pulls the chest walls inward automatically

explanation: When inspiratory muscles stop contracting, elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall naturally decreases volume to push air out. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT an accessory muscle used during forced inspiration?
explanation: The rectus femoris is a muscle in the thigh and plays no role in respiratory mechanics. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h5)

question: How do abdominal muscles assist with forced expiration?

options.A: They push abdominal organs upward to compress the chest cavity
options.B: They pull the lower ribs downward and outward simultaneously
options.C: They relax completely to allow maximum lung expansion
options.D: They hold the diaphragm firmly in a flattened position

explanation: Contraction of the abdominal wall increases intra-abdominal pressure, pushing the diaphragm higher and forcing air out quickly. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the normal resting respiratory rate range for a healthy newborn baby?
explanation: Newborns have a much faster normal breathing rate than adults, typically falling between 30 and 60 breaths per minute. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h6)

question: What physical sign should a midwife look for when assessing a newborn for respiratory distress?

options.C: Relaxed limb posture and steady heart rate

explanation: Nasal flaring and pulling in of the skin around the ribs or sternum indicate that a newborn is working extra hard to breathe. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T2#BMP121_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the main muscle that makes you breathe in during normal quiet breathing?
explanation: The diaphragm is the primary muscle that pulls air into the lungs when it tightens and moves downward. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why does air rush into your lungs when you take a breath in?

options.A: Abdominal muscles push air directly upward into the trachea
options.B: Intrapleural pressure drops below atmospheric pressure
options.C: Atmospheric pressure becomes lower than lung pressure
options.D: The chest wall actively squeezes air pockets open

explanation: Expanding the chest lowers the pressure inside the lungs compared to the outside air, making air flow inward. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which volume represents the normal amount of air inhaled or exhaled during quiet breathing?
explanation: Tidal volume is the standard amount of air moved in and out of the lungs with each normal, resting breath. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which lung volume can NEVER be measured directly using a standard handheld spirometer?
explanation: Residual volume stays inside the lungs even after blowing out as much air as possible, so it cannot be exhaled into a basic device. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which combination of volumes makes up the Vital Capacity?

options.A: Tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume
options.C: Residual volume and expiratory reserve volume
options.D: Tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, and expiratory reserve volume

explanation: Vital capacity adds together all the volumes of air a person can actively move in and out of their lungs. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h3)

question: A pregnant woman at term experiences a natural physiological reduction in which specific pulmonary capacity?
explanation: The growing uterus pushes the diaphragm up, which significantly decreases the air remaining in the lungs after a normal breath. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h3)

question: What body measurement is most closely linked to having larger lung volumes?
explanation: Taller individuals have larger chest cavities, which naturally hold more air than shorter frames. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why does lying flat on your back decrease the air left in your lungs after a normal breath?

options.A: Atmospheric pressure increases significantly at mattress level
options.B: The airways expand and lose their elastic recoil properties
options.C: Blood pools in the upper body and blocks air passages
options.D: Abdominal contents push the diaphragm upward into the chest

explanation: Gravity pulls the belly organs against the diaphragm when lying flat, which presses on the lungs and reduces resting air volume. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why are pregnant women more at risk for low blood oxygen levels when breathing becomes difficult?

options.A: The placenta absorbs all available oxygen before it reaches maternal lungs
options.B: They have increased oxygen demand combined with reduced functional residual capacity
options.C: Their red blood cells completely stop carrying oxygen during the third trimester
options.D: Their tidal volume drops to zero whenever they lie down flat

explanation: Higher body needs paired with a smaller air reserve mean pregnant women use up their oxygen stores faster. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which of the following conditions is NOT typically associated with further compromising maternal lung capacities?
explanation: Mild exercise is a normal physiological state that does not damage chest wall mechanics or restrict lung capacity like pathological conditions do. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T3#BMP121_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the main way oxygen and carbon dioxide move across cell membranes?
explanation: Gases move naturally from areas of higher pressure to areas of lower pressure without needing energy from the cells. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why does a pregnant woman's body have a higher metabolic rate?

options.A: To support the growing placenta and baby
options.B: To make up for less lung capacity late in pregnancy
options.C: To prevent excess nitrogen in the blood
options.D: To cool down the mother's body temperature

explanation: The developing baby and placenta need constant energy and support, which increases the mother's overall oxygen use. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which way do oxygen molecules naturally travel during normal breathing?

options.A: From high pressure to low pressure
options.B: From the veins into the arteries
options.C: From low pressure to high pressure
options.D: From body tissues straight into the outside air

explanation: Gas always moves down a pressure gradient, traveling from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h2)

question: How does fluid buildup in the lungs affect gas exchange?

options.A: It reverses the pressure of oxygen and carbon dioxide
options.B: It stops the heart from pumping
options.C: It forces red blood cells to release all their hemoglobin
options.D: It increases the distance gases must travel, slowing down exchange

explanation: Extra fluid creates a wider barrier between the air sacs and blood vessels, making it harder for gases to pass through quickly. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h2)

question: Where does external respiration happen in the respiratory system?

options.A: Inside the walls of the heart
options.B: Across cell membranes in body tissues
options.D: Across the air sacs in the lungs

explanation: External respiration is the gas exchange between the air in the lung alveoli and the blood in the capillaries. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is happening when a pregnant woman's body unloads carbon dioxide into her lung alveoli?

options.A: Her lungs are preparing to make more oxygen
options.B: She is getting rid of waste gas from her blood
options.C: She is storing extra carbon dioxide to balance her blood pH
options.D: Carbon dioxide is turning into solid calcium

explanation: Carbon dioxide is a waste product from cellular work. It travels through the blood to the lungs so it can be breathed out. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h3)

question: How is most oxygen carried through the bloodstream to body tissues?

options.A: Bound to hemoglobin inside red blood cells
options.C: Floating as dissolved ions in serum
options.D: Dissolved as free gas in the plasma

explanation: Hemoglobin inside red blood cells acts as the main carrier, letting the blood transport much more oxygen than plasma could on its own. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h4)

question: What does hemoglobin do when blood reaches warm, active tissues making lots of carbon dioxide?

options.A: It changes color from bright red to white
options.B: It holds onto its oxygen even tighter
options.D: It releases its stored oxygen to the tissues

explanation: Active tissues generate heat and acid, signaling hemoglobin to drop off oxygen right where it is needed most. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h4)

question: In what main form is most carbon dioxide carried back to the lungs?

options.A: As dissolved bicarbonate in the plasma
options.C: As solid crystals in the blood vessels
options.D: As gas bubbles attached to platelets

explanation: The body turns most carbon dioxide into bicarbonate so it can travel safely in the blood plasma and help control body pH. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why is turning carbon dioxide into bicarbonate important for the body?

options.A: It gives red blood cells energy to survive
options.B: It stops the liver from making too much cholesterol
options.C: It keeps blood pH within a safe range
options.D: It thickens the blood to prevent bleeding

explanation: The bicarbonate system acts as a chemical buffer, stopping blood from becoming too acidic by neutralizing extra hydrogen ions. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which way does oxygen move during internal respiration at the tissue level?

options.A: From the skin surface out into the air
options.B: From tissue cells into the lung alveoli
options.C: From venous blood into arterial circulation
options.D: From tiny blood vessels into surrounding tissue cells

explanation: Internal respiration means oxygen is being delivered from the capillaries into the working cells of the body. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which of these statements about internal respiration is FALSE?

options.A: Carbon dioxide moves from tissue cells into the blood
options.B: Oxygen levels are higher in the capillaries than in resting cells
options.C: Active tissues use up oxygen and make carbon dioxide waste
options.D: Gas exchange happens straight through the walls of the heart chambers

explanation: Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of tiny capillaries in the tissues, not through the thick muscular walls of the heart. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why does fetal hemoglobin pull oxygen away from the mother's blood in the placenta?

options.A: The placenta actively pumps oxygen using cellular energy
options.B: Maternal blood has no hemoglobin during late pregnancy
options.C: Fetal blood flows much slower than maternal blood
options.D: Fetal hemoglobin has a stronger pull on oxygen than adult hemoglobin

explanation: Fetal hemoglobin grabs onto oxygen more tightly than maternal hemoglobin, making sure the baby gets enough oxygen in the placenta. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h7)

question: What happens first to the fetus if a pregnant woman has severely low blood pressure?

options.A: Less oxygen reaches the placenta, which can cause fetal distress
options.B: The baby's birth weight and lung maturity suddenly increase
options.C: Blood flow direction in the umbilical cord reverses
options.D: Waste production stops inside the amniotic sac

explanation: Low maternal blood pressure reduces blood flow to the placenta, lowering the pressure gradient and starving the baby of needed oxygen. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h7)

question: What term describes a dangerously low level of oxygen in the mother's blood?
explanation: Hypoxemia specifically means there is a low amount of oxygen circulating in the arterial blood supply. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h8)

question: Why is placing a distressed pregnant woman on her left side a helpful nursing action?

options.A: It pushes air from her lungs straight into the placenta
options.B: It helps her bone marrow make more red blood cells
options.C: It takes pressure off major blood vessels and improves blood flow
options.D: It stops the baby from moving around in the amniotic fluid

explanation: Lying on the left side stops the heavy uterus from pressing on the inferior vena cava, keeping blood flowing well to the placenta. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T4#BMP121_U1_T4_h8)

question: Which muscles rely completely on nerve signals from the brain to contract and make breathing happen?

options.B: Elastic fibers inside the lung tissue
options.C: Cardiac muscle fibers in the atria
options.D: Smooth muscle walls of the trachea

explanation: Respiratory muscles are skeletal muscles, meaning they need neural stimulation from the brain to contract, unlike the self-exciting heart muscle. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why does the human body need a complex control system for breathing instead of just a simple fixed rhythm?

options.A: The lungs constantly change in size and shape.
options.B: Skeletal muscles tire out very quickly at rest.
options.C: Atmospheric pressure varies throughout the day.
options.D: Metabolic demands and activity levels constantly change.

explanation: The body needs a flexible system to adjust breathing depth and rate depending on whether a person is resting, active, or fighting an infection. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which part of the brainstem sets the basic rhythm for breathing?
explanation: The medullary respiratory center acts as the core pacemaker for the basic inhalation and exhalation cycle. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the main job of the pneumotaxic center in the pons?

options.A: To smooth out the transition between inhaling and exhaling
options.B: To trigger forceful coughing when dust enters the airway
options.C: To allow voluntary breath-holding during swimming
options.D: To detect low levels of oxygen directly in the blood

explanation: The pneumotaxic center limits the length of an inhalation, helping to prevent over-inflation of the lungs and keeping the breathing rhythm smooth. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h2)

question: Where are the central chemoreceptors located that monitor the brain's internal environment?
explanation: Central chemoreceptors sit right on the surface of the medulla, where they can sample the surrounding cerebrospinal fluid. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h3)

question: Why do central chemoreceptors respond more directly to changes in carbon dioxide than to changes in hydrogen ions?

options.A: Hydrogen ions are too large to move through blood vessels.
options.B: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood-brain barrier easily.
options.C: Carbon dioxide binds directly to the surface of neurons.
options.D: Hydrogen ions are completely neutral in the bloodstream.

explanation: Charged hydrogen ions cannot easily cross the blood-brain barrier, whereas gaseous carbon dioxide diffuses across rapidly to change the local fluid chemistry. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h3)

question: Which blood gas change is the most powerful normal trigger to increase breathing?
explanation: Carbon dioxide is the primary chemical regulator of normal breathing, driving increases in ventilation whenever it starts to build up. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h4)

question: A patient with severe diabetic ketoacidosis has low blood pH. How does the body compensate through breathing?

options.A: Rapid and shallow panting through an open mouth
options.B: Rapid and deep breathing to blow off carbon dioxide
options.C: Irregular gasping with long periods of no breathing
options.D: Slow and shallow breathing to retain metabolic acids

explanation: Acidosis stimulates chemoreceptors to drive deep, rapid breathing, which eliminates carbon dioxide and helps raise the blood pH back toward normal. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of the Hering-Breuer reflex in the lungs?

options.A: Slowing down the heart rate during sleep
options.B: Triggering a cough when dust enters the airway
options.C: Preventing the over-inflation of lung tissue
options.D: Stimulating oxygen absorption in the alveoli

explanation: The Hering-Breuer reflex uses stretch receptors to stop inhalation before delicate lung tissues become damaged by excessive stretching. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why does a person's breathing rate often increase the moment they start running, even before blood gas levels change?

options.A: Voluntary thought is the only cause of exercise breathing.
options.B: The heart pumps faster, forcing air into the lungs.
options.C: Proprioceptors in moving limbs signal the brainstem.
options.D: Cool outdoor air irritates the upper airways.

explanation: Neural signals from moving joints and muscles give advance notice to the respiratory centers to ramp up breathing before the body's actual metabolic needs increase. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why can giving high-flow oxygen carelessly to a patient with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) be dangerous?

options.A: It causes sudden, severe metabolic alkalosis in the blood.
options.B: It immediately destroys the delicate tissue inside the alveoli.
options.C: It blocks the brainstem from receiving any carbon dioxide signals.
options.D: It can remove their low-oxygen breathing stimulus and cause apnea.

explanation: Chronic COPD patients often rely on their low oxygen levels to stimulate breathing; sudden high oxygen tells their body that breathing is no longer necessary. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h6)

question: A woman in active labor breathes very rapidly and deeply during strong contractions. What immediate blood gas change is she most likely experiencing?

options.A: A complete failure of her peripheral chemoreceptors
options.B: A drop in carbon dioxide leading to alkalosis
options.C: A dangerous drop in arterial oxygen saturation
options.D: A massive increase in carbon dioxide causing acidosis

explanation: Rapid, deep breathing blows off excessive amounts of carbon dioxide, which reduces acid levels and raises blood pH into an alkaline state. [learn more](BMP121_U1_T5#BMP121_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the innermost layer of the gastrointestinal tract wall called?
explanation: The mucosa is the innermost layer lining the lumen of the GI tract, specialized for secretion and absorption of nutrients. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which layer of the gastrointestinal tract wall is primarily responsible for peristalsis and moving food forward?
explanation: The muscularis externa contains smooth muscle layers that contract in a wave-like motion known as peristalsis to propel food along the tract. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h1)

question: What is the name of the muscular valve that prevents stomach acid from flowing back into the esophagus?
explanation: The lower esophageal sphincter sits at the junction between the esophagus and stomach, closing tightly to keep gastric acid down. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h2)

question: A patient experiences severe heartburn due to acidic contents moving backward. Which upper GI structure has failed to close properly?
explanation: Heartburn or acid reflux happens when the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes improperly, allowing stomach acid to irritate the esophageal lining. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which of the following is NOT a part of the small intestine?
explanation: The cecum is the very first pouch-like part of the large intestine, not the small intestine. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is the main function of the large intestine in human digestion?

options.D: Beginning the mechanical chewing of food

explanation: As waste moves through the large intestine, excess water is reabsorbed back into the body, turning liquid chyme into solid stool. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h3)

question: What are the microscopic functional units of the liver called?
explanation: Hepatic lobules are the hexagonal structural and functional units that make up the internal architecture of the liver. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h4)

question: Why does the liver receive blood directly from the digestive tract through the hepatic portal vein?

options.A: To produce red blood cells for the entire body
options.B: To pump oxygen-rich blood directly back to the heart
options.C: To process absorbed nutrients and filter out toxins
options.D: To collect waste to be sent straight to the lungs

explanation: The portal system allows the liver to inspect, filter, and metabolize nutrients and toxins absorbed from the intestines before they circulate systemically. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary function of the gallbladder?
explanation: The gallbladder holds bile produced by the liver and removes water to concentrate it until it is needed for digesting fats. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which two ducts join together to form the common bile duct?

options.A: Main pancreatic duct and accessory duct
options.D: Cystic duct and common hepatic duct

explanation: The cystic duct from the gallbladder merges with the common hepatic duct draining the liver to create the common bile duct. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h5)

question: What are the hormone-producing cell clusters that make up the endocrine portion of the pancreas called?
explanation: The pancreatic islets (or islets of Langerhans) contain alpha and beta cells that release hormones like insulin and glucagon into the blood. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h6)

question: How do the exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas differ in how they release their products?

options.A: Exocrine products go through ducts into the gut, while endocrine products go straight into the blood.
options.B: Exocrine cells produce glucose, while endocrine cells produce digestive enzymes.
options.C: Exocrine organs store bile, while endocrine organs filter toxins from the liver.
options.D: Exocrine secretions control blood pressure, while endocrine secretions digest dietary proteins.

explanation: Exocrine secretions use ducts to reach the digestive tract, whereas endocrine secretions are hormones released directly into capillaries. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T1#BMP121_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of human digestion?

options.A: Breaking down food into small molecules for absorption
options.B: Storing excess vitamins in the skeletal system
options.C: Filtering waste products from the urinary bladder
options.D: Generating red blood cells for systemic circulation

explanation: Digestion turns large food items into tiny particles that can easily pass through the intestinal wall into the blood. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why must complex food molecules undergo structural changes inside the body?

options.A: Complex molecules block the normal flow of blood through organs
options.B: The stomach cannot hold solid food for more than a few minutes
options.C: Unchanged food molecules immediately trigger severe immune reactions
options.D: Large molecules are too big to cross the intestinal lining into blood

explanation: Nutrients need to be small and soluble before they can slip through the gut wall and travel to nourish body tissues. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h1)

question: What name is given to the chewed mass of food ready for swallowing?
explanation: Teeth and saliva work together in the mouth to shape chewed food into a smooth ball called a bolus. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h2)

question: How does the mechanical churning of the stomach help chemical digestion?

options.A: It neutralizes all stomach acid to protect the intestinal lining
options.B: It increases the surface area of food exposed to digestive enzymes
options.C: It freezes food particles to make them easier to dissolve
options.D: It directly converts large protein chains into individual amino acids

explanation: Breaking food into smaller physical pieces gives enzymes more exposed surface to work on, speeding up chemical breakdown. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which substance begins the chemical breakdown of starches in the oral cavity?
explanation: Saliva contains an enzyme called amylase that starts breaking down complex starches right inside the mouth. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a function of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?

options.A: Helping to denature tough protein structures in food
options.B: Providing the acidic environment required for pepsin to work
options.C: Converting complex fats directly into fatty acids without enzymes
options.D: Killing harmful bacteria swallowed along with food

explanation: Stomach acid helps activate enzymes and kill germs, but fat breakdown relies on specific lipases and bile, not acid alone. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the main role of segmentation movements in the small intestine?

options.A: Creating new enzymes to replace worn-out proteins
options.B: Back-and-forth mixing of chyme with digestive juices
options.C: Absorbing water to prevent dehydration in the colon
options.D: Pushing waste material rapidly backward toward the stomach

explanation: Segmentation sloshes chyme back and forth, ensuring thorough mixing with enzymes and contact with the gut wall. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h4)

question: What term describes the wave-like muscle contractions that move food forward?
explanation: Peristalsis involves ring-like muscles squeezing behind the food mass to push it along the digestive tract. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h4)

question: Where does the greatest amount of nutrient absorption occur in the body?
explanation: The inner lining of the small intestine is covered in tiny projections called villi, making it the primary site for absorbing nutrients. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why do many pregnant women experience sluggish digestion and heartburn during gestation?

options.A: The growing fetus completely blocks the production of all digestive enzymes
options.B: Rapid maternal weight gain destroys the villi in the small intestine
options.C: Increased stomach acid production dissolves the esophageal sphincter
options.D: Elevated progesterone levels relax smooth muscle in the digestive tract

explanation: Pregnancy hormones relax smooth muscles throughout the body, slowing down gut motility and leading to common issues like heartburn. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T2#BMP121_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which part of the gastrointestinal tract is responsible for the absorption of most nutrients?
explanation: The small intestine has specialized structures that make it the primary site for nutrient uptake in the digestive system. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the primary purpose of gastrointestinal absorption?

options.A: To move digested food into the blood or lymph
options.B: To produce digestive enzymes for the stomach
options.C: To eliminate waste products from the body
options.D: To break down large food molecules into smaller pieces

explanation: Absorption is the transfer of processed nutrients from the gut lumen into the circulatory and lymphatic systems for body use. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h1)

question: What name is given to the tiny, microscopic projections on the surface of intestinal absorptive cells?
explanation: Microvilli form a brush border on intestinal cells, which greatly increases the surface area available for taking in nutrients. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h2)

question: How do circular folds inside the small intestine help with nutrient absorption?

options.A: They produce bile acids to break down fats
options.B: They directly pump glucose across the cell membrane
options.C: They slow down the movement of digested food to allow more time for uptake
options.D: They prevent bacteria from entering the bloodstream

explanation: The circular folds cause digesting food to spiral through the tract, ensuring it stays in contact with the absorptive surface longer. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which transport process uses cellular energy to move substances against a concentration gradient?
explanation: Active transport uses energy to move molecules from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why can fat-soluble molecules pass easily through the cell membrane using simple diffusion?

options.A: Because they require specialized carrier proteins
options.B: Because they are too large to fit through pores
options.C: Because the cell membrane is made of a lipid layer
options.D: Because they must be pumped using ATP energy

explanation: Because fat-soluble substances mix well with fats, they pass easily through the fatty interior of the cell membrane without needing extra help. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the name of the packaged fat droplets that enter the lymphatic system after fat digestion?
explanation: Intestinal cells package reassembled fats with proteins into chylomicrons so they can safely enter the lymphatic vessels. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h4)

question: What role do bile salts play in the digestion and absorption of dietary fats?

options.A: They digest carbohydrates into simple sugars
options.B: They break down large fat drops into tiny droplets
options.C: They actively pump fatty acids across the brush border
options.D: They convert proteins into usable amino acids

explanation: Bile salts break large fat masses into tiny droplets, making it possible for digestive enzymes to work and for fats to be absorbed. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which substance must bind to Vitamin B12 in the stomach to enable its absorption further down the gut?
explanation: Intrinsic factor is produced by cells in the stomach and is required for Vitamin B12 absorption further down the tract. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h5)

question: How do fat-soluble vitamins get absorbed across the intestinal lining?

options.A: They cross the membrane only through endocytosis
options.B: They travel inside fat droplets and are absorbed passively
options.C: They bind exclusively to intrinsic factor in the duodenum
options.D: They require specific active transport pumps driven by ATP

explanation: Because they dissolve in fats, vitamins A, D, E, and K follow the same absorption pathway as dietary fats. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h5)

question: By what physical process does water move across the intestinal epithelium?
explanation: Water moves passively across membranes from areas of low solute concentration to high solute concentration through osmosis. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary driving force that pulls water out of the intestinal lumen?

options.A: The pumping action of the gastric glands
options.B: The pulling effect created by absorbed solutes and salts
options.C: Secretion of bile acids into the duodenum
options.D: Direct muscular contractions of the intestinal wall

explanation: As sodium and other nutrients are actively absorbed, they create an osmotic pull that draws water along with them. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which blood vessel network carries absorbed water-soluble nutrients directly to the liver?
explanation: The hepatic portal vein delivers blood containing absorbed sugars and amino acids straight to the liver for processing. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why do dietary fats enter the lymphatic system rather than directly into blood capillaries?

options.A: Because lymphatic vessels contain active pumps for lipids
options.B: Because the liver cannot process any form of dietary fat
options.C: Because digested fat particles are too large to pass through blood capillary walls
options.D: Because fat molecules are destroyed by blood enzymes

explanation: Fat particles are bulky and must enter the more permeable lacteals of the lymphatic system instead. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the term for fatty, pale, and foul-smelling stools caused by unabsorbed dietary fats?
explanation: Steatorrhea occurs when fats cannot be properly digested or absorbed, leading to high fat content in the stool. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h8)

question: A pregnant woman presents with chronic diarrhea, severe fatigue, and pale bulky stools that float. Which condition should a midwife suspect?
explanation: Fatty floating stools and fatigue point toward an inability to absorb nutrients and fats properly. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T3#BMP121_U2_T3_h8)

question: Which hormones are the main drivers of body changes and metabolism during pregnancy?
explanation: Hormones like human placental lactogen, progesterone, and estrogen drive the metabolic shifts seen in pregnant women. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why does body metabolism change significantly during pregnancy and breastfeeding?

options.A: To prevent the digestion of dietary proteins
options.B: To support fetal growth and milk production
options.C: To speed up the resting heart rate of the mother
options.D: To completely eliminate maternal fat stores

explanation: The body adapts its nutrient handling to meet the high energetic demands of the growing fetus and subsequent lactation. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h1)

question: What is the main sugar circulating in the blood that gives cells quick energy?
explanation: Glucose is the main sugar used by the body's cells for quick energy production. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h2)

question: What happens to the mother's response to insulin in late pregnancy?

options.A: Insulin sensitivity decreases to keep more sugar for the baby
options.B: Insulin sensitivity increases to clear blood sugar rapidly
options.C: All blood sugar is turned into muscle protein
options.D: The pancreas stops making insulin completely

explanation: Late pregnancy insulin resistance leaves more glucose available in the maternal blood for placental transfer. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h2)

question: Where does the body store extra dietary protein for long-term emergency use?

options.A: The body does not have a dedicated protein storage depot
options.B: Fat tissue converts it into stored albumin
options.C: Skeletal muscles store it as dense amino acid crystals
options.D: The liver stores it as specialized protein granules

explanation: Unlike fats and carbohydrates, amino acids are not stored for later use and must be continuously supplied or recycled. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h3)

question: What happens to the nitrogen part when extra amino acids are broken down for energy?

options.A: It is stored in bones to make them stronger
options.B: It is turned into urea and passed out in the urine
options.C: It is turned directly into stored muscle starch
options.D: It is breathed out through the lungs as nitrogen gas

explanation: Liver deamination removes the toxic amine group, turning it into urea so the kidneys can safely flush it out. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which food group gives the most stored energy gram for gram?
explanation: Lipids yield more than double the calories per gram compared to carbohydrates and proteins. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h4)

question: When does the liver produce higher amounts of ketone bodies?

options.A: When carbohydrate availability is very low
options.B: When protein breakdown rates exceed normal limits
options.C: Right after eating a heavy carbohydrate meal
options.D: When blood sugar levels are extremely high

explanation: Low carbohydrate availability forces the body to rely heavily on fat breakdown, leading to elevated ketone production. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which key molecule connects the breakdown pathways of carbs, proteins, and fats?
explanation: Acetyl-CoA is the key entry intermediate that feeds directly into the Krebs cycle for energy generation. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h5)

question: How does the body handle extra carbohydrates when energy needs are already met?

options.A: It destroys them through kidney filtration
options.B: It passes them out through sweat glands
options.C: It stores them as free amino acids in the blood
options.D: It turns them into fat for storage

explanation: Excess carbs that are not needed for immediate energy or glycogen storage are shifted into lipogenesis and stored as fat. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h5)

question: How does glucose mainly cross the placenta to reach the baby?
explanation: Glucose moves across the placenta down a concentration gradient using specialized carrier proteins. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the main reason metabolism shifts from storing nutrients early in pregnancy to breaking them down late in pregnancy?

options.A: To cause the mother to develop gestational diabetes
options.B: To ensure a steady fuel supply to the growing baby
options.C: To completely empty fat reserves before delivery
options.D: To stop amino acids from reaching the baby

explanation: Accelerated late pregnancy catabolism ensures the fetus gets steady nutrients even when the mother is fasting. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T4#BMP121_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which main function does the colon perform before stool reaches the rectum?
explanation: The primary role of the large intestine or colon is to extract water and mineral electrolytes from liquid waste, transforming it into formed stool. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which muscle makes up the external anal sphincter?
explanation: Unlike the internal sphincter which works automatically, the external anal sphincter is made of voluntary skeletal muscle that a person can consciously tighten or relax. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h1)

question: What happens when stool sits inside the rectum for too long without being passed?

options.A: The rectum stops sending nerve signals
options.B: It turns back into liquid chyme
options.C: More water is absorbed from it
options.D: The body digests the remaining waste

explanation: The lining of the large intestine continuously pulls water out of its contents, so delaying defecation allows more fluid to leave the stool, making it dry and hard. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h2)

question: What name is given to the strong, sweeping waves that push stool toward the rectum?
explanation: Mass movements are powerful peristaltic contractions that occur a few times a day to propel accumulated fecal waste large distances down the colon. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which part of the nervous system coordinates the powerful parasympathetic defecation reflex?
explanation: Sensory signals from the stretched rectum go to the sacral segments of the spinal cord, which then send motor signals back through pelvic nerves to drive the reflex. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h3)

question: How does the internal anal sphincter respond when the rectum fills with stool during the reflex?
explanation: The intrinsic and parasympathetic reflexes cause the smooth muscle of the internal anal sphincter to relax so that waste can move into the anal canal. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h3)

question: A postpartum mother is straining forcefully to pass hard stool. What is the main physiological effect of this straining?

options.A: Paralysis of the external anal sphincter
options.C: Decreased pressure in the chest cavity

explanation: Straining contracts the diaphragm and abdominal wall against a closed airway, which significantly raises intra-abdominal pressure to help push out stool. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which structure must consciously relax to allow intentional bowel elimination to proceed?
explanation: The external anal sphincter is made of voluntary skeletal muscle, meaning a person must consciously relax it to open the anal canal for elimination. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why are pregnant women particularly prone to developing constipation?

options.A: High progesterone levels slow bowel motility
options.B: The kidneys reabsorb all water from feces
options.C: Increased stomach acid paralyzes the colon
options.D: The liver stops producing digestive bile

explanation: Elevated progesterone relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body, including the walls of the gastrointestinal tract, which significantly slows down the movement of waste. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h5)

question: A postnatal woman on the ward is afraid to open her bowels due to perineal stitches. What initial supportive action should the midwife take?

options.A: Advise her to hold stool until the stitches heal completely
options.B: Encourage adequate fluid intake and high-fiber foods
options.C: Insist that she undergo immediate manual evacuation

explanation: Promoting natural dietary management like fluids and fiber helps soften stools gently, reducing fear and pain associated with postpartum elimination. [learn more](BMP121_U2_T5#BMP121_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for the relaxation of the smooth muscle in the ureters during pregnancy?
explanation: Progesterone circulates in high levels during pregnancy, causing smooth muscle throughout the body to relax, which leads to widening of the urinary tract. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is swelling of the kidney drainage system more common in the right ureter during pregnancy?

options.A: Progesterone receptors are found in higher concentrations on the right side.
options.B: The right renal artery exerts direct anatomical pressure on the ureter.
options.C: The pregnant uterus tilts to the right and presses on the right ureter.
options.D: The right kidney sits much lower in the abdomen than the left kidney.

explanation: The pregnant uterus usually tilts to the right, pressing the right ureter against the pelvic brim, while the sigmoid colon helps cushion the left ureter. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the name of the basic structural and functional unit of the human kidney?
explanation: Each kidney contains over a million nephrons, which are responsible for filtering blood and forming urine. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h2)

question: In which part of the kidney are the filtering units (renal corpuscles) mainly located?
explanation: The outer layer of the kidney, the cortex, houses the glomeruli and Bowman's capsules, giving it a granular texture. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h2)

question: What prevents urine from flowing backward from the bladder up into the ureters?

options.A: High negative pressure maintained inside the empty renal calyces
options.B: The angle at which the ureters pass through the bladder wall
options.C: Constant active suction exerted by the renal pelvis
options.D: Strong circular muscles located at the midpoint of each ureter

explanation: When the bladder fills, the pressure collapses the tunnel-like path of the ureter through the bladder muscle, acting as a natural valve. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT one of the three normal narrow spots along the ureter?
explanation: The ureter runs smoothly along the psoas muscle without a natural constriction; narrowings occur at the pelvis transition, pelvic vessels, and bladder entry. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the smooth triangular area on the internal floor of the urinary bladder called?
explanation: The trigone is a fixed triangular region marked by the openings of the two ureters and the urethra, remaining smooth even when the bladder empties. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h4)

question: During a difficult labor, the baby's head can press firmly in the pelvis. Which nearby organ is at the highest risk of injury due to its front position?
explanation: The urinary bladder sits directly between the pubic bones and the front wall of the uterus or vagina, making it prone to crushing injuries during difficult labor. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why are women more likely to get urinary tract infections than men?

options.A: The female urethra is much shorter and closer to the anal opening.
options.B: Progesterone prevents the immune system from protecting the female bladder.
options.C: The female bladder lacks an internal muscular valve mechanism.
options.D: The female urethral lining is composed of very fragile cells.

explanation: Bacteria from the perineum can easily travel up the short four-centimeter female urethra into the bladder. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which type of muscle forms the external urethral sphincter in the pelvic floor that allows conscious control?
explanation: The external urethral sphincter is made of voluntary skeletal muscle, allowing conscious control over urination. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h5)

question: A new mother has not passed urine six hours after a normal delivery, and her uterus feels soft and pushed to the right. What should you do first?

options.B: Insert a urinary catheter immediately without offering her the toilet.
options.C: Reassure her that holding urine for twenty-four hours after birth is normal.
options.D: Check her lower abdomen for a full bladder and help her try to pass urine.

explanation: A full bladder displaces the uterus and prevents effective contraction, leading to postpartum hemorrhage; checking for fullness and encouraging voiding is the essential first step. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is a main reason why women can have trouble emptying their bladder or get infections right after childbirth?

options.A: Permanent closure of the internal urethral sphincter
options.B: Overactivity of the bladder trigone muscle
options.C: Reduced bladder tone and increased stretch capacity after birth
options.D: Complete stopping of kidney filtration during labor

explanation: Trauma and anesthesia during childbirth temporarily reduce bladder sensation and muscle tone, predisposing women to overdistension and infection. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T1#BMP121_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the approximate total number of nephrons found inside one single healthy human kidney?
explanation: A healthy human kidney contains approximately one million nephrons working continuously to filter blood. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which of the following describes the two main parts that make up every individual nephron?

options.A: The renal corpuscle and the renal tubule
options.B: The renal pelvis and the ureter
options.D: The renal artery and the renal vein

explanation: Every nephron is built from a renal corpuscle that filters blood and a renal tubule that processes the filtrate into urine. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h1)

question: What specialized cells with foot-like extensions form filtration slits around the glomerular capillaries?
explanation: Podocytes wrap around the capillaries of the glomerulus, creating filtration slits that help block large blood cells and proteins from escaping. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h2)

question: Why is the pressure inside the glomerular capillaries much higher than in typical capillaries elsewhere in the body?

options.A: The entering arteriole is wider than the exiting arteriole
options.B: The heart pumps blood directly into the kidneys without branching
options.C: The renal veins are completely blocked by surrounding muscles
options.D: The surrounding Bowman's capsule squeezes the blood vessels tightly

explanation: The wider afferent arteriole brings blood in faster than the narrower efferent arteriole can take it out, building up the high pressure needed for filtration. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h2)

question: What microscopic feature on the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule greatly increases its surface area?
explanation: The microvilli form a brush border that maximizes the surface area for reabsorbing water and nutrients from the filtrate. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h3)

question: What happens to nearly all the glucose that is filtered out of the blood into the proximal convoluted tubule?

options.A: It is broken down into waste products and excreted
options.B: It is completely reabsorbed back into the bloodstream
options.C: It passes straight through into the final urine
options.D: It is stored inside the tubule cells as reserve fat

explanation: A healthy kidney reabsorbs almost 100 percent of filtered glucose back into the blood in the proximal convoluted tubule so none is lost in the urine. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which part of the Loop of Henle is freely permeable to water but does NOT let salt pass out?
explanation: The descending limb allows water to move out into the salty medulla while keeping solutes trapped inside, concentrating the fluid. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary role of the thick ascending limb of the Loop of Henle?

options.A: Adding large protein waste molecules to the filtrate
options.B: Reabsorbing all remaining glucose and amino acids
options.C: Actively pumping out salt without letting water follow
options.D: Slowing down the flow of urine to rest the kidney

explanation: The ascending limb pumps out ions like sodium and chloride to create the medullary concentration gradient while remaining impermeable to water. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h4)

question: Which hormone acts on the distal convoluted tubule to increase the reabsorption of sodium ions?
explanation: Aldosterone targets the distal nephron to promote sodium retention and potassium excretion, helping maintain blood volume and pressure. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h5)

question: How does antidiuretic hormone (ADH) affect the cells of the collecting duct when a person is dehydrated?

options.A: It thickens the tubule walls to prevent any fluid from passing through
options.B: It blocks salt pumps to make the urine completely salt-free
options.C: It stops all filtration in the glomerulus to save body fluids
options.D: It causes water channels to be inserted, letting water leave the tubule

explanation: ADH triggers the insertion of aquaporins, allowing water to escape the collecting duct back into the body, resulting in concentrated urine. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which microscopic structure is primarily damaged during glomerulonephritis?

options.A: The simple squamous cells of the renal pelvis
options.B: The glomerular basement membrane and podocytes
options.C: The smooth muscle lining the ureter walls
options.D: The collecting duct aquaporin water channels

explanation: Glomerulonephritis involves inflammation and injury to the filtration barrier of the glomerulus, leading to protein and blood in the urine. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h6)

question: Why does acute tubular necrosis cause a sharp drop in urine production?

options.A: All water is absorbed back into the bloodstream instantly
options.B: The glomerulus stops receiving blood from the renal artery entirely
options.C: Dead tubule cells break off and block the inside of the tubule
options.D: The bladder muscles become paralyzed by toxins

explanation: When tubule cells die in acute tubular necrosis, they detach and plug the tubular lumen, preventing urine from flowing through properly. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T2#BMP121_U3_T2_h6)

question: What is the main functional unit of the kidney that filters blood and makes urine?
explanation: The nephron is the microscopic unit inside the kidney responsible for filtering blood and producing urine. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h1)

question: What is the main job of the glomerulus in the kidney?

options.A: It stores finished urine temporarily before it travels down the ureter
options.B: It acts as a high-pressure capillary bed for filtering blood
options.C: It secretes large amounts of concentrated urea directly into the bladder
options.D: It produces the hormone erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell growth

explanation: The glomerulus is a cluster of capillaries that uses blood pressure to filter water and small particles out of the blood. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h1)

question: What primary force pushes fluid across the glomerular membrane during filtration?
explanation: Blood pressure inside the glomerular capillaries pushes water and small solutes through the filtration membrane. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h2)

question: A pregnant patient's lab results show red blood cells and large proteins in her urine. Which part of her nephron is likely damaged?
explanation: Healthy filtration membranes keep blood cells and large proteins inside the blood vessels. Finding them in urine indicates a breakdown in this barrier. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h2)

question: In which part of the nephron does the greatest amount of tubular reabsorption happen?
explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs most of the filtered water, glucose, and nutrients back into the bloodstream. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h3)

question: Why does water follow reabsorbed sodium out of the renal tubules?

options.A: Active water pumps push fluid across the cell membrane
options.B: Osmosis pulls water toward areas of higher solute concentration
options.C: Hydrostatic pressure builds up in the tubular lumen
options.D: Specialized cilia sweep water molecules into capillaries

explanation: When active transport moves sodium out of the tubule, water follows passively by osmosis to balance solute concentrations. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h3)

question: What is the direction of movement for substances during tubular secretion?

options.A: From the loop of Henle into the interstitial tissue
options.B: From the collecting duct into the renal pelvis
options.C: From Bowman's capsule into the glomerulus
options.D: From peritubular capillaries into the renal tubules

explanation: Tubular secretion moves waste products from the surrounding blood vessels directly into the nephron tubules for removal. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a main goal of tubular secretion?

options.A: Excreting metabolic waste products and drug metabolites from circulation
options.B: Clearing excess potassium ions to prevent dangerous heart rhythms
options.C: Regulating the acid-base balance of the body by eliminating hydrogen ions
options.D: Reabsorbing 100 percent of filtered glucose back into the blood

explanation: Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, whereas tubular secretion focuses on eliminating waste and balancing acids and ions. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h4)

question: How do the descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle differ?

options.A: The descending limb is active, while the ascending limb is entirely passive
options.B: The descending limb lets water out, while the ascending limb pumps out salt
options.C: The descending limb secretes acid, while the ascending limb absorbs glucose
options.D: Both limbs allow free passage of all salts and large proteins

explanation: The descending limb allows water to leave by osmosis, while the ascending limb pumps out salt without letting water follow. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h5)

question: Which hormone acts on the collecting duct to control water reabsorption and urine concentration?
explanation: Antidiuretic hormone manages the permeability of the collecting duct to water, helping the body conserve water when needed. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h5)

question: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks has trace glucose in her urine, but normal blood sugar. What is the likely reason?

options.A: She is experiencing acute kidney failure caused by undiagnosed preeclampsia
options.B: Increased GFR during pregnancy can exceed the tubular reabsorption limit for glucose
options.C: The loop of Henle has failed to establish a proper medullary gradient
options.D: Her renal tubules have completely stopped functioning due to severe infection

explanation: Pregnancy increases the rate of kidney filtration, which can sometimes push more glucose into the tubules than they can fully reabsorb. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h6)

question: What significant condition is indicated by persistent protein in the urine during routine antenatal checks?
explanation: Proteinuria in pregnancy points to changes in the filtration barrier and serves as a key warning sign for preeclampsia. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T3#BMP121_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is the main goal of fluid and electrolyte regulation in the body?

options.A: Preventing the digestion of excess dietary proteins
options.B: Maintaining stable water volume and chemical composition
options.C: Slowing down cellular metabolism during resting states
options.D: Increasing the total amount of waste produced daily

explanation: The body keeps water and chemical levels within safe limits so that cells can work normally. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h1)

question: Why is understanding fluid balance especially important when caring for pregnant women?

options.A: Kidneys shut down entirely during the second trimester of gestation
options.B: Electrolyte levels never fluctuate at any point during normal gestation
options.C: Pregnancy causes massive shifts in maternal blood volume and fluid handling
options.D: Pregnant women completely stop losing water through normal respiration

explanation: Expectant mothers experience large changes in total body water, which makes them sensitive to fluid and electrolyte shifts. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h1)

question: Which fluid compartment holds the largest percentage of total body water in an adult?
explanation: About two-thirds of total body water is stored inside the cells as intracellular fluid. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which of the following is the main electrolyte found inside body cells?
explanation: Potassium is the major positive ion found inside cells, while sodium is more common outside the cells. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h2)

question: What is the main working unit of the kidney that filters blood and makes urine?
explanation: The nephron is the microscopic unit in the kidney that handles filtering, reabsorbing, and making urine. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h3)

question: How do healthy kidneys respond when a person becomes very dehydrated?

options.A: They convert excess waste directly into solid mineral crystals
options.B: They produce a small volume of highly concentrated urine
options.C: They flush large amounts of water out through the bladder
options.D: They stop filtering blood entirely until fluid intake occurs

explanation: To save water when the body is dry, the kidneys reabsorb as much water as possible, making urine concentrated and small in volume. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h3)

question: Which hormone helps the kidneys reabsorb water back into the body?
explanation: Antidiuretic hormone signals the kidney collecting ducts to let water pass back into the bloodstream, reducing urine output. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h4)

question: What triggers the adrenal glands to release aldosterone?

options.A: High blood volume stretching the heart muscle
options.B: Low blood pressure or low sodium levels
options.C: Excessive water intake during heavy exercise
options.D: Elevated blood sugar levels after a heavy meal

explanation: When blood pressure or sodium drops, the body releases aldosterone to help hold onto salt and water. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which electrolyte imbalance poses the most immediate danger to heart rhythm?
explanation: Potassium is vital for heart muscle stability, so abnormal levels can quickly disrupt heartbeats. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why are normal sodium levels so important for brain function?

options.A: Sodium acts as the primary energy source for brain cell mitochondria
options.B: Sodium shifts determine extracellular fluid volume and cellular osmolality
options.C: Sodium molecules form the structural scaffolding of neurons
options.D: Sodium directly prevents the buildup of urea inside brain tissue

explanation: Changes in blood sodium cause water to move in or out of brain cells, leading to swelling or shrinking that affects brain function. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is the normal pH range for arterial blood in humans?
explanation: Normal arterial blood pH is kept strictly between 7.35 and 7.45 to keep body chemistry working properly. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h6)

question: How do the kidneys respond when a patient develops severe metabolic acidosis (too much acid)?

options.A: They excrete large amounts of bicarbonate into the urine and hold acid
options.B: They stop producing urine entirely to trap all acids in the tissues
options.C: They secrete more hydrogen ions into the urine and reabsorb bicarbonate
options.D: They rely exclusively on the lungs to fix the pH without renal changes

explanation: To fix acidosis, the kidneys pump extra acid into the urine while keeping bicarbonate in the blood to balance the pH. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h6)

question: A woman in her third trimester has mild ankle swelling after standing for a long time. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Complete absence of antidiuretic hormone secretion
options.B: Total renal failure caused by high dietary salt intake
options.C: Compression of pelvic veins by the enlarging uterus
options.D: Severe intracellular dehydration of all lower limb tissues

explanation: The heavy uterus presses on pelvic blood vessels, slowing blood return from the legs and causing normal ankle swelling. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a normal fluid change during the postpartum period?

options.A: Sweating or excessive sweating to shed fluid
