options.C: Rapid diuresis of excess extracellular fluid volume
options.D: Permanent suppression of all kidney filtration

explanation: Kidney filtration does not shut down; postpartum fluid loss happens through heavy urination and sweating. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T4#BMP121_U3_T4_h7)

question: What is the main smooth muscle that forms the wall of the urinary bladder?
explanation: The detrusor muscle is the primary smooth muscle of the bladder wall. It stretches as the bladder fills and contracts to push urine out during voiding. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why does the detrusor muscle need to relax significantly while the bladder is storing urine?

options.A: To allow the bladder to hold urine without a high pressure increase
options.B: To push urine upward toward the kidneys continuously
options.C: To open the internal urethral sphincter automatically
options.D: To stimulate the pudendal nerve to close the external sphincter

explanation: Relaxing the detrusor muscle lets the bladder expand and hold more urine while keeping pressure low, which protects the upper urinary tract. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which nerve pathway supplies the main signal for the bladder to contract when passing urine?
explanation: Parasympathetic fibers running through the pelvic splanchnic nerves stimulate the detrusor muscle to contract so the bladder can empty. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h2)

question: What is the main role of the sympathetic nervous system on the bladder while it is storing urine?

options.A: Sending pain signals directly to the cerebral cortex during filling
options.B: Triggering immediate bladder emptying when it reaches half capacity
options.C: Relaxing the external urethral sphincter to allow continuous dripping
options.D: Promoting urine retention by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the sphincter

explanation: Sympathetic activity takes over during the storage phase to keep the bladder relaxed and the internal sphincter firmly closed. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h2)

question: At about what volume does an adult bladder usually trigger the initial urge to pass urine?
explanation: The stretch receptors in a normal adult bladder trigger the micturition reflex when volume reaches about 300 to 400 mL. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h3)

question: Why do newborn babies wet themselves constantly without conscious control?

options.A: The micturition reflex is purely spinal and lacks adult higher brain modulation
options.B: The kidneys produce too much urine relative to body size
options.C: The external urethral sphincter is permanently paralyzed in infants
options.D: The detrusor muscle lacks the ability to contract on its own

explanation: Infant nervous systems are not yet fully matured, meaning the brain cannot yet override the basic spinal reflex that empties the bladder automatically. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h3)

question: Which specific part of the brainstem acts as the main coordination center for passing urine?
explanation: The pontine micturition center coordinates the relaxation of the sphincters and the contraction of the detrusor muscle for smooth urination. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h4)

question: A patient has a spinal cord injury above the sacral region but below the brainstem. What is the usual long-term bladder outcome?

options.A: Total permanent inability to ever produce urine
options.B: Complete lack of any bladder sensation or contraction forever
options.C: Normal voluntary control restored within a few days
options.D: Automatic reflex voiding without voluntary cerebral control

explanation: When brain control is blocked by a spinal injury, the lower spinal reflex arc remains intact, causing the bladder to empty automatically by reflex. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h4)

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for relaxing the smooth muscle of the urinary tract during pregnancy?
explanation: Progesterone causes smooth muscles throughout the body to relax, which affects the ureters and bladder during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h5)

question: Why is a full bladder after childbirth a major concern for the midwife regarding postpartum hemorrhage?

options.A: Infection spreads rapidly to cause severe uterine atony
options.B: It causes immediate rupture of the external urethral sphincter
options.C: The retained urine directly dilutes circulating clotting factors
options.D: A full bladder displaces the uterus and prevents effective uterine contraction

explanation: A distended bladder pushes the uterus out of position, stopping it from contracting firmly to clamp down on blood vessels after delivery. [learn more](BMP121_U3_T5#BMP121_U3_T5_h5)

question: What do we call glands that release their secretions directly into the bloodstream without using ducts?
explanation: Endocrine glands do not have ducts to carry their secretions, releasing hormones straight into nearby blood vessels instead. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why is it important for midwives to understand the endocrine system when caring for pregnant women?

options.A: Hormones produced by endocrine glands are only active during the first trimester of gestation
options.B: The endocrine system operates completely independently of the reproductive system during pregnancy
options.C: Midwives spend most of their training performing surgical removal of diseased endocrine organs
options.D: Pregnancy and childbirth involve massive hormonal shifts that regulate labor and postpartum recovery

explanation: Maternal adaptations and the actual process of labor rely heavily on coordinated hormone releases from multiple glands. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h1)

question: In which bony structure of the skull does the pituitary gland sit?
explanation: The sella turcica is a saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone that houses and protects the pituitary gland. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h2)

question: What is the main difference between the front (anterior) and back (posterior) lobes of the pituitary gland?

options.A: The posterior lobe controls basal metabolic rate, while the anterior lobe regulates only uterine contractions
options.B: The posterior lobe produces oxytocin independently, while the anterior lobe has no endocrine function
options.C: The anterior lobe synthesizes its own hormones, while the posterior lobe stores and releases hypothalamic hormones
options.D: The anterior lobe connects directly to the optic chiasm, while the posterior lobe sits outside the skull

explanation: Oxytocin and ADH are manufactured in the hypothalamus and simply stored and released by the posterior pituitary, unlike anterior hormones. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h2)

question: Where are the parathyroid glands located in relation to the thyroid gland?

options.A: Inside the central isthmus of the thyroid
options.B: On the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes
options.C: Deep within the cartilage of the larynx
options.D: Superior to the hyoid bone in the upper neck

explanation: Usually numbering four, the small parathyroid glands are embedded or attached directly to the back of the thyroid gland lobes. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h3)

question: If the parathyroid glands are accidentally damaged or removed during thyroid surgery, what immediate problem is the patient at risk of developing?

options.A: Severe low blood calcium leading to muscle tetany
options.B: Sudden enlargement of the anterior pituitary gland
options.C: Uncontrollable spikes in maternal blood pressure
options.D: Complete cessation of all thyroid hormone production

explanation: Parathyroid hormone controls calcium levels; losing these glands causes blood calcium to drop dangerously low, affecting nerve and muscle function. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h3)

question: In which part of the abdomen are the adrenal glands located?
explanation: The adrenal glands sit directly on top of the kidneys, placing them behind the peritoneal lining in the retroperitoneal space. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the hormones produced by the adrenal cortex?

options.A: Supporting metabolic processes alongside other endocrine organs
options.B: Regulating salt and water balance through mineralocorticoids
options.C: Helping the body manage physical and emotional stress via cortisol
options.D: Triggering the rapid fight-or-flight response during sudden fright

explanation: The fight-or-flight response is mediated by adrenaline and noradrenaline, which are secreted by the inner adrenal medulla, not the cortex. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h4)

question: What are the tiny clusters of hormone-producing cells scattered throughout the pancreas called?
explanation: The endocrine pancreas is made up of these tiny cell clusters containing alpha and beta cells that regulate blood sugar. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why is the pancreas considered a mixed or dual-purpose gland?

options.A: It produces hormones that affect both the anterior pituitary and the adrenal cortex
options.B: It has both exocrine tissue for digestion and endocrine tissue for hormone release
options.C: It functions independently during pregnancy but requires the liver to work postpartum
options.D: It is located partially inside the peritoneal cavity and partially within the skull

explanation: The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes via ducts (exocrine) and hormones directly into the blood (endocrine). [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h5)

question: Where are the female ovaries typically located?

options.A: Attached directly to the posterior pituitary gland
options.B: In the pelvic cavity lateral to the uterus
options.C: Within the anterior neck inferior to the larynx
options.D: In the retroperitoneal space above the kidneys

explanation: The ovaries sit on either side of the uterus in the true pelvis, securely held by supportive ligaments. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why are the male testes located outside the main body cavity in the scrotum?

options.A: To maintain a lower temperature required for healthy sperm production
options.B: To ensure the rapid synthesis of adrenal cortex steroid hormones
options.C: To allow direct connection with the exocrine ducts of the pancreas
options.D: To protect the pelvic organs from the pressure of the growing uterus

explanation: Scrotal placement keeps the testes slightly cooler than core body temperature, which is essential for spermatogenesis. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h6)

question: Which major endocrine gland is situated in the front of the neck just below the voice box?
explanation: The thyroid gland wraps around the front of the trachea in the lower neck, just under the larynx. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h7)

question: A pregnant client is diagnosed with gestational diabetes. Which organ and hormone system are primarily involved in this condition?

options.A: Posterior pituitary and its blocked oxytocin release
options.B: Pancreas and its inadequate insulin production
options.C: Adrenal cortex and its deficient cortisol output
options.D: Thyroid gland and its excess thyroxine secretion

explanation: Gestational diabetes involves problems with blood sugar regulation tied to insulin produced by the endocrine pancreas. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T1#BMP121_U4_T1_h7)

question: What fluid do endocrine glands use to send their hormones directly to target organs?
explanation: Endocrine glands do not have ducts. They release hormones directly into the blood circulation so they can travel throughout the body. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h1)

question: How do hormone signals from the endocrine system generally compare to nerve signals from the nervous system?

options.A: Nervous system actions are permanent whereas hormones are temporary
options.B: Endocrine responses are slower and longer lasting
options.C: Nervous responses rely on circulating chemical messengers
options.D: Endocrine impulses travel exclusively along nerve fibres

explanation: Chemical signals traveling through the blood take longer to start than electrical nerve impulses, but their effects usually last much longer. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which brain structure is the main connection between the nervous and endocrine systems?
explanation: The hypothalamus picks up nerve signals and turns them into hormone signals by controlling the nearby pituitary gland. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h2)

question: A woman has weak contractions during the third stage of labor. Which hypothalamic hormone helps strengthen these contractions?
explanation: Oxytocin is released from the back part of the pituitary gland and attaches to uterine muscle to help create strong contractions. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which nutrient from our diet is needed to make thyroid hormones?
explanation: Thyroid hormones need iodine atoms to form, making a diet with enough iodine essential for their production. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h3)

question: What is the main job of parathyroid hormone in the body?

options.D: To stimulate sodium retention in the kidneys

explanation: Parathyroid hormone responds to low blood calcium by drawing calcium from bones, helping the kidneys keep more of it, and increasing absorption in the gut. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which hormone tells the kidneys to hold onto sodium and get rid of potassium?
explanation: Aldosterone is made by the outer part of the adrenal glands and helps the kidneys balance fluids and electrolytes. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT something adrenaline normally does during a sudden stress event?
explanation: Adrenaline actually opens up the airways in the lungs to let in more oxygen during stress, rather than tightening them. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which specific cells in the pancreas make and release insulin?
explanation: Beta cells produce and release insulin when blood sugar levels go up after eating carbohydrates. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h5)

question: A patient feels dizzy and sweats after missing a meal. Which hormone goes to work to raise their blood sugar?
explanation: When blood sugar drops between meals, alpha cells release glucagon to tell the liver to break down stored glycogen and release sugar. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which hormone found in early urine or blood tests lets us know a woman is pregnant?
explanation: hCG is produced by the early placenta right after implantation, and it is the hormone standard pregnancy tests look for. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the main job of progesterone during pregnancy?

options.A: To trigger the immediate onset of active labor contractions
options.B: To stimulate early follicle development in the ovaries
options.C: To maintain the uterine lining and keep the myometrium relaxed
options.D: To promote direct milk ejection from the mammary ducts

explanation: Progesterone keeps the muscles of the uterus calm and relaxed throughout pregnancy to protect the baby from early birth. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h6)

question: How does a negative feedback loop usually work in the endocrine system?

options.A: It prevents target organs from ever responding to circulating signals
options.B: It suppresses further hormone secretion when blood levels become too high
options.C: It destroys circulating hormones directly inside the bloodstream
options.D: It amplifies hormone release continuously until an external event stops it

explanation: Negative feedback slows down or stops hormone production when levels get high, bringing the body back to its normal balance point. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h7)

question: Which of these is a classic example of positive feedback in human reproduction?

options.A: Oxytocin release causing contractions that push the baby against the cervix
options.B: Thyroid hormones reducing the production of TSH from the pituitary gland
options.C: Aldosterone stopping sodium excretion when blood pressure drops
options.D: Insulin lowering blood glucose levels after eating a carbohydrate meal

explanation: When the baby presses against the cervix, it triggers more oxytocin release, which causes stronger contractions, pushing the baby harder against the cervix in a building loop. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T2#BMP121_U4_T2_h7)

question: What main chemical messengers does the endocrine system use to coordinate body functions?
explanation: The endocrine system uses hormones released directly into the bloodstream to reach and regulate distant target organs. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is keeping hormone levels within a steady range important for the body?

options.A: To stop external changes from affecting the skin
options.B: To make nervous system impulses travel faster
options.C: To maintain internal balance and prevent stress on the body
options.D: To prevent red blood cell production from stopping

explanation: Keeping hormone levels balanced protects the body from the harmful effects of having too much or too little of a specific chemical. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h1)

question: What is the main job of a negative feedback loop in the endocrine system?

options.A: To reverse a change and restore normal balance
options.B: To turn chemical signals into fast electrical impulses
options.C: To permanently stop hormone production in all glands
options.D: To amplify a stimulus until a physical event finishes

explanation: Negative feedback works by counteracting a change, bringing the internal environment back to its normal baseline. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h2)

question: What happens when a hormone level gets too high in a standard negative feedback system?

options.A: The nervous system takes over the gland completely
options.B: The gland is stimulated to produce even more hormone
options.C: Target organs stop responding to all chemical signals
options.D: Secretion of that hormone is slowed down to lower levels

explanation: High levels of a hormone signal the body to stop releasing more, keeping amounts safe and balanced. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which of the following describes how a positive feedback loop works?

options.A: It turns slow hormonal signals into quick reflexes
options.B: It works to return a fluctuating variable to a steady set point
options.C: It blocks all communication between the brain and organs
options.D: It builds up the original stimulus to drive a process forward

explanation: Positive feedback builds on the initial change, pushing the system forward to complete a specific goal like childbirth. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why does the body use positive feedback loops much less often than negative feedback loops?

options.A: Hormones in positive feedback cannot travel in the blood
options.B: Positive feedback only works during childhood
options.C: Unchecked positive feedback can cause dangerous runaway effects
options.D: Positive feedback requires too much nervous system energy

explanation: Because positive feedback keeps increasing a response, it needs a clear stopping point to avoid harming the body. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which part of the brain releases hormones to control the anterior pituitary gland?
explanation: The hypothalamus produces control hormones that travel to the anterior pituitary to direct its releases. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the main benefit of having a multi-step pathway involving the hypothalamus, pituitary, and other glands?

options.A: To stop the brain from receiving signals from organs
options.B: To make hormone levels increase continuously without stopping
options.C: To skip the bloodstream and use direct nerve pathways
options.D: To allow precise control over circulating hormone levels

explanation: Having multiple checkpoints helps the body finely adjust and control hormone output with high accuracy. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h4)

question: A midwife gives synthetic oxytocin to strengthen weak contractions during labour. Which natural body process is this supporting?

options.A: A positive feedback loop involving cervical stretch and hormone release
options.B: A hypothalamic shutdown of the pituitary gland
options.C: A negative feedback loop that lowers blood pressure
options.D: A steady hormone release that ignores uterine stretching

explanation: Synthetic oxytocin helps the natural positive feedback loop where contractions stretch the cervix, releasing more natural oxytocin. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why must midwives pay close attention to thyroid hormone levels in early pregnancy?

options.A: The thyroid stops responding to pituitary signals during pregnancy
options.B: Thyroid hormones work entirely through positive feedback during gestation
options.C: The developing baby relies on maternal thyroid hormones before its own gland works
options.D: Maternal thyroid levels drop to zero right after conception

explanation: Early baby development depends on the mother's thyroid hormones, making normal endocrine function vital for healthy growth. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T3#BMP121_U4_T3_h5)

question: What chemical messengers do endocrine glands use to send signals through the body?
explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream to reach distant target organs and help keep the body in balance. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h1)

question: In a negative feedback loop, what happens when hormone levels get too high?

options.A: The releasing gland is forced to make even more hormone.
options.B: The controlling gland is signaled to slow down hormone production.
options.C: The liver stores the excess hormone molecules.
options.D: Target cells destroy the circulating hormone.

explanation: Negative feedback works like a thermostat, slowing hormone release when levels rise to keep the body stable. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h1)

question: Where does the problem lie in a primary endocrine disorder?

options.D: Directly within the target gland itself

explanation: A primary disorder means the specific organ responsible for making the hormone is diseased or damaged. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which lab result points to a primary gland failure rather than a secondary issue?

options.A: Low stimulating hormone and low target hormone
options.B: High stimulating hormone and low target hormone
options.C: Normal stimulating hormone and high target hormone
options.D: High stimulating hormone and high target hormone

explanation: When a target gland fails, the brain sends out extra stimulating hormone to force a response, resulting in high tropic hormone and low target hormone levels. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which of these is a common cause of too much hormone production in the body?
explanation: Noncancerous growths on endocrine tissue often pump out excess hormones without listening to the body's normal feedback signals. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h3)

question: Why does having too many hormones often lead to sudden physical exhaustion or weight changes?

options.A: It pushes the body's metabolic rate into overdrive.
options.B: It blocks the absorption of all dietary proteins.
options.C: It causes severe retention of heavy body fluids.
options.D: It completely stops the production of digestive enzymes.

explanation: Excess metabolic hormones speed up cellular activity so fast that the body burns through energy stores much faster than usual. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h3)

question: How does pregnancy affect the mother's endocrine system?

options.A: It lowers overall hormone production to protect the baby.
options.B: It places higher demands on maternal glands to work harder.
options.C: It prevents any hormonal changes from happening.
options.D: It temporarily shuts down the pituitary gland.

explanation: Pregnancy requires maternal organs to step up their work to supply hormones for both the mother and the growing baby. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h4)

question: Why is a lack of maternal thyroid hormone especially risky during early pregnancy?

options.A: It prevents the placenta from attaching.
options.B: It causes immediate paralysis in the mother.
options.C: The baby relies entirely on the mother's thyroid hormone before its own gland starts working.
options.D: It triggers rapid weight gain that affects the pelvis.

explanation: During the first trimester, the baby depends completely on maternal thyroid hormones for healthy brain development and growth. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h4)

question: Why should lab results be interpreted carefully in pregnant women?

options.A: Pregnancy destroys all circulating hormones in the blood.
options.B: Labor contractions interfere with chemical lab tests.
options.C: Fetal blood mixes completely with maternal plasma.
options.D: Pregnancy changes normal blood volume and hormone-binding proteins.

explanation: Normal physical changes during pregnancy mean standard lab ranges can look abnormal unless interpreted with pregnancy in mind. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the main goal of a dynamic function test on an endocrine gland?

options.A: To remove small noncancerous tumors without surgery
options.B: To check if the gland responds properly to stimulation or suppression
options.C: To measure the physical size of the gland using ultrasound
options.D: To check if the patient's diet contains enough iodine

explanation: Dynamic tests use specific substances to challenge the gland and see if its feedback system is working correctly. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h5)

question: Which healthcare professional is usually responsible for routine antenatal checks and spotting early warning signs?
explanation: Midwives provide ongoing antenatal care, putting them on the front line to catch early signs of endocrine complications. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h6)

question: What should a midwife do if a pregnant patient on thyroid medication reports new heart palpitations and tremors?

options.A: Advise her to increase her daily salt intake
options.B: Refer her promptly for a medical review and possible dose adjustment
options.C: Tell her to stop taking her medication right away
options.D: Reassure her that this is normal third-trimester fatigue

explanation: Palpitations and tremors can mean the hormone dose is too high or the condition is changing, which needs a doctor's evaluation. [learn more](BMP121_U4_T4#BMP121_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the main job of the nervous system during labor contractions?

options.A: Releasing surfactant into the fetal lungs
options.B: Producing amniotic fluid inside the uterus
options.C: Filtering maternal blood through the kidneys
options.D: Coordinating uterine contractions and pain perception

explanation: The nervous system processes pain signals from the uterus and works with hormones like oxytocin to manage labor. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for a midwife to know basic brain and nerve function when caring for a patient with eclampsia?

options.C: It allows the midwife to repair cranial nerves
options.D: It explains the nervous system irritation that causes seizures

explanation: Eclampsia involves nervous system overactivity that leads to convulsions, so understanding neural pathways helps with emergency care. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h1)

question: Which two main structures make up the Central Nervous System?
explanation: The central nervous system consists simply of the brain inside the skull and the spinal cord protected by the backbone. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h2)

question: What is the main job of the Peripheral Nervous System in relation to the Central Nervous System?

options.A: It acts as the communication link between the CNS and the rest of the body
options.B: It destroys tired neurotransmitters before they reach the spine
options.C: It is where conscious thoughts are created
options.D: It makes cerebrospinal fluid to cushion the brain

explanation: Peripheral nerves carry sensory messages to the brain and spinal cord, and carry motor instructions back out to the muscles and organs. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h2)

question: What are the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord called?
explanation: The meninges are three layers of tissue that protect the brain and spinal cord from injury. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h3)

question: How does the spinal cord protect the body from sudden injury?

options.A: By storing extra sugar for emergency muscle use
options.B: By pumping oxygen through the spine
options.C: By handling quick reflex actions without waiting for the brain

explanation: Spinal reflexes allow the body to react instantly to danger by sending signals straight through the spinal cord to the muscles. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h3)

question: How many pairs of cranial nerves branch directly from the brain?
explanation: There are twelve pairs of cranial nerves that handle senses and movement around the head, face, and neck. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h4)

question: When a midwife checks a newborn's sucking and rooting reflexes, which group of nerves is mainly being tested?
explanation: Facial movements, swallowing, and feeding reflexes are controlled by cranial nerves coming from the brainstem. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h4)

question: Which part of the nervous system gives a mother conscious control over her muscles when pushing during labor?
explanation: The somatic nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscles, allowing the mother to push effectively. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h5)

question: What is the main role of the sympathetic nervous system during physical stress?

options.A: Producing voluntary hand and foot movements
options.B: Triggering the fight or flight response for emergencies
options.C: Stimulating digestion and normal gland function
options.D: Slowing down the heart rate to save energy

explanation: The sympathetic system prepares the body for action by speeding up the heart rate and releasing stored energy. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h5)

question: During a Caesarean section done with spinal anesthesia, which part of the nervous system is temporarily blocked to stop pain?

options.B: Spinal nerves in the subarachnoid space
options.D: Somatic motor fibers in the arms

explanation: Spinal anesthesia blocks nerve roots in the spinal fluid, stopping pain signals from traveling up to the brain. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h6)

question: Why does a midwife check newborn reflexes and muscle tone during the first physical exam?

options.A: To measure the baby's total blood volume
options.C: To determine the infant's future intelligence
options.D: To check for signs of nervous system depression or birth trauma

explanation: Normal reflexes and muscle tone show that the newborn's nervous system is healthy and working properly after birth. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T1#BMP121_U5_T1_h6)

question: What two main organs make up the central nervous system?
explanation: The central nervous system is specifically defined as comprising the brain and the spinal cord, which together process all incoming and outgoing neural signals. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why do midwives need a basic understanding of the nervous system?

options.B: To help spot conditions like eclampsia and birth defects
options.C: To diagnose community mental health disorders

explanation: Midwives monitor nervous system health to catch complications early, such as pregnancy-induced seizures and spinal development issues. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT one of the three main parts of the brain?
explanation: The spinal cord runs down the back as a separate pathway, while the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem make up the brain itself. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h2)

question: What is the main job of the spinal cord in connection with the brain?

options.A: Filtering waste products from nerve tissue
options.D: Acting as a signal highway between the body and the brain

explanation: The spinal cord carries messages from the body up to the brain, and sends movement commands back down from the brain to the body. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which part of the brain is mainly responsible for balance and smooth movement?
explanation: The cerebellum focuses on fine-tuning muscle movements and keeping posture and balance steady during physical activities. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h3)

question: A newborn baby shows unsteady movements and poor muscle control. Which brain area is likely still developing or affected?
explanation: Because the cerebellum coordinates movement and balance, issues in this region often show up as uncoordinated physical activity in infants. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h3)

question: What vital body function does the brainstem manage automatically without thinking?
explanation: The brainstem controls essential life-support functions like breathing and heart rhythm without needing conscious effort. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h4)

question: Why is severe injury to the brainstem considered an immediate medical emergency?

options.A: It prevents a person from balancing on one leg
options.B: It makes the feet lose their sense of touch
options.C: It controls basic survival functions like breathing
options.D: It stops a person from speaking clearly

explanation: Damage to the brainstem disrupts vital processes such as breathing and heartbeat, causing rapid danger to the whole body. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h4)

question: What do ascending nerve tracts in the spinal cord carry?

options.C: Movement commands away from the brain

explanation: Ascending nerve tracts act as pathways that carry touch and pain signals up from the body to the brain for processing. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h5)

question: What happens when a section of the spinal cord is badly damaged?

options.D: Signals between the brain and body are blocked below the injury

explanation: Spinal cord injuries break the nerve pathways, stopping sensory and movement signals from passing the injured spot. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h5)

question: What are the three protective membrane layers covering the brain and spinal cord called?
explanation: The dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater make up the meninges, which wrap around and protect the central nervous system. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is one of the main jobs of cerebrospinal fluid?

options.A: Cushioning the brain against physical shocks
options.B: Pumping oxygen into red blood cells
options.C: Digesting proteins in the spinal canal

explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid acts as a liquid cushion, protecting delicate brain and spinal tissues from bumps and impacts. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is the term for a birth defect where the spinal column fails to close properly during early growth?
explanation: Spina bifida happens when the embryonic neural tube around the spinal cord does not close completely during development. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h7)

question: A pregnant woman at 34 weeks has a severe headache, blurry vision, and sudden convulsions. Which nervous system complication is she most likely experiencing?
explanation: Sudden seizures or convulsions in a pregnant woman with signs of pre-eclampsia point to eclampsia, a serious nervous system emergency. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T2#BMP121_U5_T2_h7)

question: What are the two main functional divisions of the peripheral nervous system?
explanation: The peripheral nervous system splits into the somatic division for voluntary actions and the autonomic division for involuntary body processes. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which of the following functions is primarily controlled by the somatic nervous system during childbirth?

options.A: Automatic constriction of maternal blood vessels
options.B: Voluntary contraction of the abdominal skeletal muscles
options.C: Spontaneous acceleration of the maternal heart rate
options.D: Involuntary dilation of the uterine cervix

explanation: Somatic nerves control voluntary skeletal muscles, which a mother uses consciously when pushing during labor. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h1)

question: Name the cranial nerve responsible for transmitting visual information from the eye to the brain.
explanation: Cranial nerve II is the optic nerve, which is solely dedicated to carrying visual signals from the retina. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h2)

question: Why is cranial nerve X, the vagus nerve, uniquely important compared to many other cranial nerves?

options.A: It emerges from the lower spinal cord rather than directly from the base of the brain.
options.B: It handles all special senses including sight, hearing, taste, and smell simultaneously.
options.C: It is the only cranial nerve that controls voluntary movements of the skeletal limbs.
options.D: It extends beyond the head and neck to regulate internal organs like the heart and gut.

explanation: Unlike most cranial nerves that stay in the head area, the vagus nerve travels downward to influence thoracic and abdominal organs. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h2)

question: Through which spinal cord root do incoming sensory nerve signals enter the central nervous system?
explanation: The dorsal root of a spinal nerve contains sensory nerve fibers bringing information from the body toward the spinal cord. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h3)

question: A laboring woman receives an epidural block for pain relief. Which primary nerve structures are directly affected by the local anesthetic to stop pain transmission?
explanation: An epidural targets spinal nerves as they exit the spinal cord, blocking pain signals coming from the lower body and uterus. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of a neurological reflex arc in the human body?

options.A: To slow down bodily responses during periods of deep relaxation
options.B: To produce rapid, involuntary responses to protect or regulate the body
options.C: To store long-term memories within peripheral nerve pathways
options.D: To allow the brain time to consciously analyze complex intellectual problems

explanation: Reflex arcs bypass conscious processing to create instant, automatic reactions that protect the body from harm. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h4)

question: Why do midwives test primitive reflexes like rooting and sucking in a healthy newborn baby?

options.A: To train the baby to digest breast milk without experiencing colic
options.B: To check if the infant's cranial and spinal nerve pathways are functioning properly
options.C: To measure the exact weight and length of the newborn child accurately
options.D: To determine the infant's future intelligence and cognitive development

explanation: Checking newborn reflexes helps midwives ensure that the baby's peripheral and central nervous systems are intact and working. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard reason for a midwife to assess nerve function?

options.A: To check for signs of postpartum neurological complications
options.B: To measure the exact gestational age of an unborn fetus
options.C: To identify nerve compression injuries caused by prolonged labor
options.D: To monitor recovery from spinal anesthesia after a cesarean birth

explanation: Nerve assessments check nervous system health, not fetal age, which is determined through ultrasound or last menstrual period. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h5)

question: A postpartum mother complains of numbness and weakness in one leg after a long, difficult labor. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Permanent damage to the primary olfactory cranial nerve
options.B: Sudden failure of the autonomic nervous system to regulate blood
options.C: Temporary compression of lumbosacral nerve roots by the baby's head
options.D: Infection of the central brain tissue caused by high fever

explanation: Extended pressure from the fetal head during a difficult labor can temporarily press on nearby spinal nerve roots, causing localized leg numbness. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T3#BMP121_U5_T3_h5)

question: Which body activities does the autonomic nervous system control?

options.B: Sensory perception of sharp skin pain

explanation: The autonomic nervous system handles automatic body processes without conscious direction. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why is maintaining homeostasis the main goal of the autonomic nervous system?

options.A: It prepares the skeletal muscles for heavy exercise
options.B: It stops all organ activity during times of deep sleep
options.C: It speeds up digestion whenever a person feels stressed
options.D: It keeps internal body conditions stable and balanced

explanation: The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions balance each other to keep the body's internal environment stable. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h1)

question: Where do the early nerve fibers of the sympathetic nervous system start?

options.A: Thoracolumbar region of the spinal cord
options.B: Skeletal muscle tissue fibers in the limbs
options.C: Craniosacral region of the central nervous system
options.D: Cerebral cortex of the frontal brain lobe

explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies are found specifically in the thoracic and upper lumbar spinal segments. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h2)

question: How do parasympathetic nerve pathways generally compare to sympathetic ones?

options.A: Parasympathetic pathways possess very short preganglionic nerve fibers
options.B: Parasympathetic pathways do not use any form of ganglionic synapses
options.C: Parasympathetic pathways originate entirely within the lumbar spinal cord
options.D: Parasympathetic pathways have long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibers

explanation: Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers travel a long distance to reach ganglia situated right next to or inside the target organ. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h2)

question: What happens in the body when the sympathetic nervous system is activated?

options.C: Constriction of the pupil of the eye
options.D: Increased blood flow to the gut

explanation: Sympathetic activation widens the airways to allow more oxygen entry during high-energy states. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h3)

question: A labouring woman is feeling very frightened and anxious. Which bodily response is expected from her sympathetic nervous system?

options.A: Faster heart rate and elevated blood pressure
options.B: Increased digestive activity and heavy salivation
options.C: Immediate constriction of her pupils in bright light
options.D: Enhanced blood flow shifting strictly to her intestines

explanation: Fear triggers the sympathetic fight-or-flight response, which speeds up the heart and raises blood pressure. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h3)

question: What is the main job of the parasympathetic nervous system?

options.B: Preparing the body for sudden physical combat
options.C: Triggering massive adrenaline release into blood
options.D: Spiking blood glucose levels for fast running

explanation: The parasympathetic division manages resting functions, energy storage, and digestion. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h4)

question: How do parasympathetic responses differ from sympathetic responses in the body?

options.A: Parasympathetic pathways always use short preganglionic fibers
options.B: Parasympathetic effects are localized rather than generalized body-wide reactions
options.C: Parasympathetic nerves directly stimulate skeletal muscle contraction
options.D: Parasympathetic activation stops all metabolic activity entirely

explanation: Parasympathetic fibers stimulate individual organs separately, unlike the widespread mass activation of the sympathetic system. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h4)

question: Which chemical messenger is released by all autonomic preganglionic nerve fibers?
explanation: Acetylcholine is the chemical messenger used at all autonomic ganglia by preganglionic fibers of both systems. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h5)

question: Where are muscarinic receptors typically found in the autonomic nervous system?

options.A: At synapses inside the sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia
options.B: On target organs of the parasympathetic nervous system
options.C: Inside the central nervous system preganglionic cell bodies
options.D: Directly on the cell membranes of skeletal muscle fibers

explanation: Muscarinic receptors respond to acetylcholine at parasympathetic effector tissues, whereas nicotinic receptors sit on ganglia. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h5)

question: What does 'dual innervation' mean for an organ?

options.A: It is controlled entirely by conscious somatic motor pathways
options.B: It possesses two separate hearts beating at different rates
options.C: It receives nerve fibers from both sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
options.D: It uses both acetylcholine and adrenaline at the exact same receptor

explanation: Dual innervation means an organ gets inputs from both parts of the autonomic nervous system to finely tune its function. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following body parts is an exception because it usually receives ONLY sympathetic nerve supply?

options.B: The smooth muscle of the stomach
options.C: The muscular wall of the heart
options.D: The circular iris muscle of the eye

explanation: Most blood vessels and sweat glands rely solely on sympathetic tone for regulation rather than dual input. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h6)

question: How can high anxiety and fear negatively affect a woman's progress in labour?

options.A: Sympathetic overactivation can reduce uterine blood flow and slow contractions
options.B: Excessive acetylcholine release causes immediate exhaustion of skeletal muscles
options.C: Parasympathetic dominance instantly stops all cervical dilation permanently
options.D: Vagal nerve stimulation completely prevents any sensation of uterine pain

explanation: Fear triggers sympathetic fight-or-flight activity, releasing hormones that divert blood from the uterus and can impede labour progress. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h7)

question: A midwife keeps the labour room quiet, dims the lights, and speaks softly to a stressed mother. What is the main physiological goal of this care?

options.A: To force a rapid switch to sympathetic fight-or-flight status
options.B: To block all sensory nerve pathways coming from the pelvis
options.C: To reduce sympathetic activity and encourage relaxation
options.D: To stimulate nicotinic receptors inside the autonomic ganglia

explanation: A calm, soothing environment reduces maternal stress and dampens excess sympathetic tone, aiding normal labour physiology. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T4#BMP121_U5_T4_h7)

question: Which part of the neuron receives incoming signals from other cells?
explanation: Dendrites are the branched extensions of a neuron that act like antennae to pick up chemical and electrical messages from neighboring cells. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h1)

question: What is the main job of the myelin sheath along an axon?

options.A: To connect the dendrites directly to the cell nucleus
options.B: To insulate the fiber and speed up electrical impulse travel
options.C: To manufacture neurotransmitters for chemical synapses
options.D: To anchor the neuron firmly within muscle tissue

explanation: Myelin acts as an insulation layer around the nerve fiber, preventing signal loss and helping electrical impulses travel much faster. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h1)

question: What is the typical electrical charge inside a resting neuron?
explanation: When a neuron is at rest, its internal charge sits at about -70 mV, making the inside more negative than the outside. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h2)

question: How do sodium-potassium pumps maintain the resting charge of a cell?

options.A: By pumping sodium out and potassium into the cell using energy
options.B: By balancing calcium and chloride ions without using energy
options.C: By destroying excess potassium ions inside the cytoplasm
options.D: By allowing sodium to flood inward freely through open gates

explanation: The sodium-potassium pump uses cellular energy to continuously push three sodium ions out and pull two potassium ions in to keep the resting state stable. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h2)

question: Which ion rushes into the neuron when an impulse first starts?
explanation: When a nerve signal starts, special channels open up and allow sodium ions to rush inside, changing the cell charge from negative to positive. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h3)

question: What happens if a stimulus is too weak to reach the threshold of -55 mV?

options.A: A very slow action potential travels down the axon
options.B: No action potential will be generated at all
options.C: The cell permanently loses its resting potential
options.D: Only potassium channels open to create a small spike

explanation: Nerve signals follow an all-or-none rule. If the stimulus does not reach the -55 mV threshold, the neuron simply does not fire. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h3)

question: Why does the absolute refractory period prevent a second nerve impulse right away?

options.A: The myelin sheath has melted away completely
options.B: Potassium pumps have stopped working permanently
options.C: The cell has run out of all water molecules

explanation: During the absolute refractory period, the sodium channels take a brief break and enter an inactive state where they cannot open again immediately. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of the refractory period in nerve transmission?

options.A: Producing extra neurotransmitters for the next cell
options.B: Speeding up the movement of ions across the axon
options.C: Ensuring impulses travel in only one direction
options.D: Keeping the resting membrane potential permanently positive

explanation: By making the recently fired part of the axon temporarily unresponsive, the refractory period ensures the nerve signal moves forward and does not double back. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h4)

question: What are the tiny gaps in the myelin sheath where nerve signals actually occur called?
explanation: The exposed spaces between segments of the myelin sheath are called nodes of Ranvier, and they contain high concentrations of ion channels. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h5)

question: How does saltatory conduction affect the speed of a nerve impulse?

options.A: It slows down the signal so the brain can process it clearly
options.B: It makes the impulse travel much faster by jumping between nodes
options.C: It converts the electrical signal into a purely chemical hormone
options.D: It stops the signal entirely until energy is replenished

explanation: Saltatory conduction lets the electrical signal leap quickly from one node of Ranvier to the next, speeding up transmission significantly. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h5)

question: What is the tiny space between two communicating neurons called?
explanation: The synaptic cleft is the microscopic gap between the end of one neuron and the start of the next cell. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h6)

question: What role does calcium play when a nerve impulse reaches the end of an axon?

options.A: It triggers vesicles to release neurotransmitters into the cleft
options.B: It destroys excess myelin to allow direct cell contact
options.C: It converts the nerve cell into a muscular fiber
options.D: It immediately stops all electrical activity in the neuron

explanation: When calcium enters the end of the axon, it causes tiny storage sacs to release chemical messengers into the synaptic space. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h6)

question: How do local anesthetics like lidocaine help relieve pain during an episiotomy repair?

options.A: By increasing the resting potential to make firing easier
options.B: By dissolving the myelin sheath surrounding motor neurons
options.C: By blocking voltage-gated sodium channels to stop pain signals
options.D: By destroying neurotransmitters inside the spinal cord

explanation: Lidocaine stops pain by blocking sodium channels, which prevents nerve cells from firing and sending pain signals to the brain. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT related to nerve physiology in obstetric care?

options.A: Using magnesium sulfate to calm central nervous system irritability in eclampsia
options.B: Calculating the exact daily caloric intake required for fetal bone growth
options.C: Applying local anesthetics for pain relief during perineal tear repair
options.D: Administering epidural anesthesia to block pain pathways during labor

explanation: Caloric intake and fetal bone development deal with nutrition and growth, not nerve signal transmission. [learn more](BMP121_U5_T5#BMP121_U5_T5_h7)

question: What is the main job of the true pelvis during childbirth?

options.A: Acting as the bony birth canal for the baby
options.B: Supporting the entire weight of the upper spine
options.C: Anchoring the major muscles of the lower thighs
options.D: Protecting the kidneys and upper abdominal organs

explanation: The true pelvis sits below the pelvic brim and forms the rigid channel that the fetus navigates during labor. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why is the bony pelvis shaped like a basin?

options.A: To allow the developing fetus to float freely in the abdominal cavity
options.B: To increase the total volume of fluid inside the pregnant uterus
options.C: To prevent any movement whatsoever in the lower half of the body
options.D: To effectively transfer upper body weight and protect reproductive organs

explanation: Its ring-like, basin shape provides structural strength while housing and shielding delicate internal pelvic structures. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which three bones join together to form each hip bone?
explanation: During childhood and growth, the ilium, ischium, and pubis fuse at the acetabulum to create a single hip bone on each side. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is the name of the small, tail-like bone at the bottom of the sacrum?
explanation: The coccyx is the terminal segment of the spinal column and provides a slight amount of movement during fetal descent. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h2)

question: What causes the pelvic joints to become loose and movable during pregnancy?

options.A: Rapid stretching of the overlying skin
options.B: Increased calcium deposits in the cartilage
options.C: The release of pregnancy hormones like relaxin
options.D: Direct pressure from the heavy fetal head

explanation: Hormones produced during gestation specifically target pelvic ligaments and joints to prepare the pelvis for childbirth. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h3)

question: Where is the pubic symphysis located in the pelvis?

options.A: At the very bottom tip of the tailbone
options.B: On the upper wing of the iliac crest
options.C: At the front, joining the two pubic bones
options.D: At the back, connecting the spine to the hip

explanation: The pubic symphysis sits right at the front middle, uniting the left and right pubic bones. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which ligament runs from the sacrum to the ischial spine?
explanation: The sacrospinous ligament spans horizontally from the lateral border of the sacrum and coccyx to the prominent ischial spine. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the main role of the pelvic ligaments during pregnancy and labor?

options.A: To produce the hormones that soften the cervix before delivery
options.B: To actively push the baby down through the birth canal during contractions
options.C: To limit excessive movement of the pelvic bones while allowing necessary stretch
options.D: To completely lock the joints so no movement can occur

explanation: Ligaments provide structural stability, preventing the pelvis from over-separating while still permitting slight give during birth. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h4)

question: What anatomical landmark marks the boundary between the false and true pelvis?
explanation: The pelvic brim acts as the dividing line separating the upper false pelvis from the lower true pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which of the following describes the false pelvis?

options.A: It lies above the pelvic brim and supports the pregnant uterus
options.B: It forms the rigid, narrow bony canal for fetal descent
options.C: It is bounded below by the pelvic outlet and perineum
options.D: It contains the ischial spines used to measure engagement

explanation: The false pelvis is part of the abdominal cavity framework, holding abdominal contents and the expanding uterus. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h5)

question: During a vaginal examination in labor, a midwife feels the ischial spines. What are these landmarks used to assess?

options.A: Checking the degree of cervical effacement
options.B: Estimating the total amniotic fluid volume
options.C: Determining the station of the presenting fetal part
options.D: Measuring the exact blood pressure of the mother

explanation: The ischial spines represent zero station, serving as the crucial reference point for how far the baby has descended into the pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized pelvic shape in obstetrics?
explanation: The four classic pelvic shapes are gynecoid, android, anthropoid, and platypelloid; pyramidal is not one of them. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T1#BMP210_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which part of the pelvis forms the actual birth canal during childbirth?
explanation: The true pelvis lies below the pelvic brim and houses the actual birth canal through which the baby passes. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why do pelvic joints become more mobile during pregnancy?

options.A: The growing baby physically forces the bones apart
options.B: Hormones like relaxin loosen the ligaments
options.C: Calcium leaves the bones to feed the baby
options.D: Increased muscle tone pulls the joints open

explanation: Pregnancy hormones soften the pelvic ligaments to slightly expand the birth canal for delivery. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h1)

question: What is the average measurement of the transverse diameter of the pelvic brim?
explanation: The transverse diameter is the widest transverse span of the pelvic brim, measuring roughly 13 centimetres. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h2)

question: When a midwife measures the diagonal conjugate during an examination, what is she trying to estimate indirectly?
explanation: The diagonal conjugate is measured with fingers to estimate the true obstetric conjugate, which cannot be reached directly. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h2)

question: What structural feature of the pelvis causes the baby to curve forward as it moves down the birth canal?

options.A: The prominent ischial spines in the mid-pelvis
options.B: The movable coccyx at the pelvic outlet
options.C: The wide transverse diameter of the pelvic brim
options.D: The short front wall and long back wall

explanation: The shallow pubic bone in front combined with the deep sacrum in the back forces the baby to curve forward during descent. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is the main role of the Curve of Carus during active labour?

options.A: It guides the natural curved path the baby follows to be born
options.B: It prevents the umbilical cord from wrapping around the baby's neck
options.C: It protects the maternal bladder from pressure
options.D: It determines whether an episiotomy is necessary

explanation: The baby rotates along this curved pathway, which matches the natural shape of the birth canal from top to bottom. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which measurement represents the transverse diameter of the pelvic outlet?
explanation: The bisischial diameter measures the distance between the two ischial tuberosities at the pelvic outlet. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why is a wide subpubic angle important during the second stage of labour?

options.A: It reduces the risk of postpartum haemorrhage
options.B: It allows the placenta to deliver faster
options.C: It prevents premature rupture of the membranes
options.D: It gives the foetal head enough space to pass under the pubic arch

explanation: A wide subpubic angle permits safe extension and crowning of the baby's head beneath the pubic bone. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h4)

question: At what anatomical landmark is the foetal head considered to be at Station 0 during internal examination?
explanation: The plane of the ischial spines marks station zero, indicating that engagement has occurred. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h5)

question: A first-time mother at 39 weeks presents with a high, unengaged baby's head despite regular contractions. What condition should the midwife suspect first?
explanation: Failure of engagement at term in a first-time mother often points toward a potential mismatch between the baby's head and the pelvic brim. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T2#BMP210_U1_T2_h5)

question: About what percentage of women have the classic gynecoid pelvis?
explanation: Roughly half of all women possess this classic pelvic shape, which makes it the most common female pelvic type. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why is the gynecoid pelvis considered the most favorable type for childbirth?

options.A: It forces the baby to deliver much faster than normal
options.B: It guarantees that the placenta will deliver before the baby
options.C: It completely prevents any possibility of perineal tearing
options.D: Its rounded shape offers smooth internal space for the baby to pass through

explanation: The open, rounded shape provides ample room at every level of the pelvis, reducing barriers during labour. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h1)

question: How do the ischial spines typically feel in a normal gynecoid pelvis?
explanation: In a gynecoid pelvis, the ischial spines are typically rounded and blunt, meaning they do not block the descending baby's head. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h2)

question: What shape is the pelvic inlet in a gynecoid pelvis?

options.D: A rounded or slightly oval shape

explanation: The inlet is wide and rounded, giving the baby's head plenty of room to enter the birth canal. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the average measurement of the front-to-back diameter at the pelvic inlet?
explanation: The true conjugate or front-to-back diameter of the inlet measures roughly 11 centimetres in a normal gynecoid pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h3)

question: If a woman has a roomy gynecoid pelvis, what does this mean for the baby during labour?

options.A: The baby's head will remain unengaged until pushing begins
options.B: The baby will experience immediate shoulder dystocia at the inlet
options.C: The baby will find it easy to turn its head inside the pelvis
options.D: The baby is forced to stay in a breech position

explanation: A roomy mid-pelvis with good side-to-side space supports smooth internal rotation of the baby's head during the second stage of labour. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h3)

question: In what position does the baby's head usually enter the inlet of a gynecoid pelvis?
explanation: The wide side-to-side diameter of the gynecoid inlet makes the transverse position the most natural way for the head to enter. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why is it rare for a baby's head to be too large for a pure gynecoid pelvis?

options.A: All internal measurements are large enough to let a normal-sized baby pass
options.B: The baby's head shrinks automatically upon entering the pelvis
options.C: The amniotic fluid cushions the baby against tight spaces
options.D: The pelvic bones are softer and stretch apart during pregnancy

explanation: Cephalopelvic disproportion happens when the baby's head is too big for the pelvis, which is unlikely in a roomy gynecoid structure. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h4)

question: Where does the back of the baby's head (occiput) rotate toward during internal rotation in a gynecoid pelvis?

options.B: Toward the pubic bone at the front
options.C: Toward the left ischial spine only
options.D: Toward the hollow of the tailbone

explanation: During internal rotation, the occiput moves forward to lie underneath the pubic arch for birth. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h5)

question: What movement helps the baby's head pass out from under the pubic arch during birth?
explanation: As the head reaches the perineum, it extends upwards and outwards underneath the pubic arch to deliver the face and chin. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which clinical assessment helps estimate the front-to-back diameter of the pelvic inlet?

options.D: Checking the distance between the sitting bones

explanation: The diagonal conjugate is assessed manually during a vaginal examination to help estimate the clearance of the pelvic inlet. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is a major advantage of manual pelvic assessment in everyday midwifery practice?

options.A: It can be performed quickly at the bedside without expensive machinery
options.B: It replaces the need for tracking contractions
options.C: It provides exact millimetre measurements of the baby's skull
options.D: It prevents all forms of prolonged labour

explanation: Manual pelvimetry is a practical, low-cost bedside skill that gives immediate clues about pelvic shape in resource-limited settings. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T3#BMP210_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is another common name for the android pelvis?
explanation: The android pelvis closely resembles the typical male pelvic skeleton due to its narrow and heavy bony structures. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is identifying an android pelvis useful during pregnancy care?

options.A: To determine the exact birth weight of the baby
options.B: To prevent the baby from turning into a breech position
options.C: To prescribe specific diets that widen the pelvic bones
options.D: To anticipate labor challenges and plan safe delivery

explanation: Early identification allows midwives to monitor labor closely and prepare for possible support if passage becomes difficult. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h1)

question: What shape describes the pelvic inlet of an android pelvis?
explanation: The promontory of the sacrum and the converging side walls push inward, creating a characteristic wedge or heart shape at the inlet. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h2)

question: How do the ischial spines usually feel during a vaginal examination in an android pelvis?

options.A: Completely flat and impossible to feel
options.D: Soft and movable under gentle pressure

explanation: Prominent, sharp, and inward-pointing ischial spines reduce the space of the midpelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which shape best describes the overall internal passage of the android pelvis?
explanation: The pelvis narrows steadily from top to bottom, resembling a kitchen funnel which can make descent tighter for the baby. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is true about the transverse diameter of the pelvic inlet in an android pelvis?

options.A: It remains completely equal from front to back
options.B: It expands significantly during the second stage of labor
options.C: It is narrow near the front and wide near the back
options.D: It is wide near the front and narrow near the back

explanation: The wedge shape pushes the widest transverse portion backward toward the sacrum, leaving little space at the front of the pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why might the fetal head fail to engage easily in an android pelvis?

options.A: The front of the pelvis is too narrow for the baby's head
options.B: The amniotic fluid volume is lower than normal
options.C: The maternal abdominal muscles are too weak
options.D: The umbilical cord wraps around the neck early

explanation: The narrow wedge at the front prevents the baby's head from fitting comfortably into the inlet during late pregnancy. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which fetal position is frequently associated with the mechanics of an android pelvis?
explanation: The posterior positioning allows the smaller diameters of the fetal head to adapt better to the wedge-shaped pelvic inlet. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h4)

question: A woman with an android pelvis shows no progress in labor for two hours despite strong contractions. What is the most appropriate midwifery action?

options.A: Administer oral pain medication and wait another four hours
options.B: Perform fundal pressure to push the baby through
options.C: Encourage the woman to lie flat on her back to rest
options.D: Escalate for medical review and possible caesarean section

explanation: When a narrow pelvis causes labor to stop, surgical intervention is necessary for safety. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary tool used by midwives to monitor the progress of labor and detect delays early?
explanation: The partograph provides a pictorial overview of labor progress, helping midwives recognize prolonged labor before complications worsen. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T4#BMP210_U1_T4_h5)

question: What is the shape of the pelvic inlet in an anthropoid pelvis?

options.A: A wide oval from side to side
options.D: A long oval from front to back

explanation: The anthropoid pelvis is shaped like an oval where the front-to-back measurement is longer than the side-to-side measurement. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why does a midwife need to identify an anthropoid pelvis during pregnancy?

options.A: To know if the mother needs a blood transfusion
options.C: To figure out the exact gestational age of the fetus
options.D: To understand how the baby will move through the birth canal

explanation: Knowing the pelvic shape helps midwives anticipate how labor will progress and spot any mechanical challenges early. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which bone feature is commonly found in an anthropoid pelvis?

options.B: A side-to-side inlet wider than the front-to-back
options.D: A short sacrum with four segments

explanation: The anthropoid pelvis typically features prominent ischial spines that can narrow the middle part of the pelvic cavity. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h2)

question: How does the sacrum usually look in an anthropoid pelvis?
explanation: The sacrum in this pelvic type is long and narrow, which makes the pelvic cavity deeper from front to back. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which pelvic measurement is longer at the inlet of an anthropoid pelvis?
explanation: The main feature of the anthropoid inlet is a front-to-back diameter that is longer than the side-to-side diameter. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h3)

question: A woman with an anthropoid pelvis has a narrow side-to-side inlet. How does the baby's head usually enter the pelvis?

options.A: The baby stays floating until the last stage of labor
options.D: Engagement happens above the brim without any alignment

explanation: Because side-to-side space is limited, the fetal head enters the pelvis aligned with the long front-to-back path. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h3)

question: Which fetal position is more common in an anthropoid pelvis than in a standard round pelvis?
explanation: The narrow shape of the anthropoid pelvis means babies are found in the occipitoposterior position much more often during labor. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is a common effect of narrow side-to-side dimensions during labor?

options.A: The baby travels down in a front-to-back alignment
options.C: A rapid birth without any skull molding
options.D: The shoulders come out before the head

explanation: The restricted side-to-side room forces the fetus to travel down the birth canal using the long front-to-back axis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why is a patient, watchful approach recommended during the second stage of labor in an anthropoid pelvis?

options.A: The placenta separates too early in this pelvis type
options.C: Oxytocin drips are banned for first-time mothers
options.D: Labor can take longer due to the deep cavity and posterior positions

explanation: A deeper pelvis and posterior positions require extra time for the baby to descend, so patience prevents unnecessary medical interventions. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a safe first step when managing a posterior baby position in an anthropoid pelvis?

options.A: Monitoring the baby's heart rate closely
options.B: Using a vacuum extractor before the cervix is fully open
options.C: Encouraging the mother to change positions

explanation: Instrumental delivery is never performed before the cervix is fully dilated, regardless of the shape of the pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T5#BMP210_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is another common name for the platypelloid pelvis?
explanation: The platypelloid pelvis is widely known as the flat pelvis because of its characteristic compressed shape. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h1)

question: How do the main diameters of a platypelloid pelvic inlet compare to each other?

options.A: The anteroposterior diameter is wide while the transverse diameter is reduced
options.B: Both the transverse and anteroposterior diameters are unusually long
options.C: Both the transverse and anteroposterior diameters are equally shortened
options.D: The transverse diameter is wide while the anteroposterior diameter is reduced

explanation: This pelvic type is defined by a shortened front-to-back measurement paired with a broad side-to-side measurement. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which feature is typically observed at the inlet of a platypelloid pelvis?
explanation: The defining skeletal trait at the pelvic inlet of this type is a reduced front-to-back measurement. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h2)

question: What shape does the pelvic inlet usually take in a platypelloid pelvis?
explanation: The flattening of the inlet creates a broad, kidney-like or wide oval outline. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which nutritional deficiency is historically linked to bone softening that causes a flat pelvis?
explanation: A lack of vitamin D leads to rickets, which weakens growing bones and can cause them to deform under body weight. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h3)

question: How does childhood bone softening contribute to a platypelloid shape?

options.A: Premature fusion of the hip bones stops vertical growth
options.B: Downward pressure from the spine flattens the weakened pelvic brim
options.C: Excessive leg pulling widens the outlet sideways
options.D: Lack of muscle tone shrinks the sacral bone entirely

explanation: When soft bones bear weight, the vertical force pushes the sacrum forward and flattens the pelvic ring. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h3)

question: How must the baby's head typically engage in a platypelloid pelvis due to the inlet shape?
explanation: The wide transverse diameter forces the baby's head to enter the pelvis sideways. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h4)

question: A woman with a confirmed platypelloid pelvis is in active labour, and the fetal head remains high and unengaged at 39 weeks. What is the midwife's primary concern?

options.A: Fetopelvic disproportion due to the narrow inlet
options.B: Rapid precipitous delivery through a wide midcavity
options.C: Early rupture of membranes from a deep sacral curve
options.D: Umbilical cord knotting caused by excessive space

explanation: The reduced front-to-back space often prevents the head from fitting through the inlet, creating a mechanical block. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which clinical measurement is typically used to estimate the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet?
explanation: The diagonal conjugate is measured during a vaginal examination to help gauge the front-to-back room at the pelvic inlet. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h5)

question: Why is routine X-ray pelvimetry largely avoided in modern antenatal care for suspected platypelloid pelvis?

options.A: X-ray machines cannot detect the difference between a flat pelvis and a normal gynecoid pelvis
options.B: Pelvic bones change shape so rapidly during pregnancy that measurements become useless
options.C: Radiation causes immediate malformation in the developing fetal brain
options.D: Clinical observation during a trial of labour combined with ultrasound is generally preferred over radiation exposure

explanation: Modern practice minimises radiation risks to the fetus, relying instead on clinical exams and careful monitoring of labour progress. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T6#BMP210_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary shape of the pelvic floor muscle sling?
explanation: The pelvic floor is formed like a funnel, sloping downward and inward to support the pelvic organs while allowing structures like the urethra, vagina, and rectum to pass through. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why is the structural integrity of the pelvic floor important for pelvic organs?

options.A: It produces hormones that regulate the menstrual cycle
options.B: It prevents intra-abdominal pressure from pushing organs downward
options.C: It completely seals the pelvic cavity to block all fluid movement
options.D: It actively pumps blood back up to the heart from the uterus

explanation: The muscles and fascia of the pelvic floor act as a physical hammock, counteracting gravity and downward pressures from the abdominal cavity to keep organs in their proper place. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which specific muscle group of the levator ani forms a sling directly behind the rectum?
