explanation: The puborectalis muscle loops behind the rectum to create an angle that helps maintain fecal continence until relaxed. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h2)

question: A postpartum woman is taught pelvic floor exercises to improve urinary control. Which muscle is she primarily contracting?
explanation: Pelvic floor exercises target the levator ani muscle group, which surrounds the urethra and vagina, helping to restore tone and continence after birth. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h2)

question: Where is the perineal body anatomically located in the female pelvis?

options.B: Behind the rectum against the sacrum
options.C: Between the vagina and the anus
options.D: Within the broad ligament of the uterus

explanation: The perineal body sits right in the middle between the lower vagina and the anal canal, acting as a meeting point for pelvic floor muscles. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h3)

question: Why is the perineal body considered a crucial structural node during normal vaginal delivery?

options.A: It cuts off blood supply to the lower vagina to limit bleeding
options.B: It secretes lubricating fluids to ease the passage of the baby's shoulders
options.C: It acts as a central anchoring point where multiple pelvic muscles meet
options.D: It pushes the baby's head directly upward toward the pubic bone

explanation: Because many muscles converge here, the perineal body holds the pelvic floor together and absorbs a great deal of stretching force during delivery. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the primary function of the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments?

options.A: To close the vaginal opening during non-pregnant states
options.B: To supply oxygenated blood to the pelvic floor muscles
options.C: To connect the pubic bone directly to the tailbone
options.D: To suspend and anchor the cervix and upper vagina

explanation: These fascial ligaments provide the main suspension system that keeps the uterus and upper vagina from sagging downward into the pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h4)

question: What clinical condition usually results when endopelvic fascia and ligaments weaken significantly?
explanation: When the fascial hammock and supporting ligaments lose their strength, organs like the bladder, uterus, or rectum can drop out of their normal positions. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h4)

question: How do the levator ani muscles help direct the mechanism of labor as the baby descends?

options.A: They contract forcefully to push the baby out without maternal effort
options.B: They seal the cervix shut until crowning occurs
options.C: They absorb all amniotic fluid to keep the birth canal dry
options.D: Their slope helps guide the fetal head to rotate forward

explanation: The downward and forward slope of the resting pelvic floor acts like a slide, helping the presenting part rotate correctly toward the front of the pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which hormone helps soften the connective tissues of the pelvis in preparation for labor?
explanation: Relaxin, along with other hormones, helps loosen pelvic ligaments and soft tissues so they can stretch during childbirth. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which degree of perineal tear involves the anal sphincter muscles but not the rectal mucosa?
explanation: A third-degree tear involves injury to the perineal muscles and the anal sphincter complex, while fourth-degree tears also tear through the rectal lining. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h6)

question: A woman who recently had a forceps-assisted vaginal delivery experiences long-term pelvic floor weakness. Which specific injury is a common cause of this?

options.A: Levator ani avulsion from the pubic bone
options.B: Necrosis of the uterine cervical os
options.C: Complete rupture of the pubic symphysis bone
options.D: Atrophy of the abdominal rectus muscles

explanation: Rapid stretching or instrumental deliveries can tear the levator ani muscle completely away from its bony attachment on the pubis, causing lasting weakness. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T7#BMP210_U1_T7_h6)

question: Why is checking the pelvis so important in Nigerian midwifery practice?

options.A: Calculating the precise gestational age of the fetus
options.B: Determining the exact birth weight of the baby
options.D: Preventing obstructed labor and maternal complications

explanation: Assessing the pelvis helps spot space limitations early, which prevents prolonged and obstructed labor that can harm the mother and baby. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h1)

question: What is a common reason why some young women develop a narrowed or contracted pelvis?

options.A: Excessive physical exercise during early adolescence
options.B: Frequent use of tight traditional waist beads
options.C: High consumption of calcium-rich local foods
options.D: Childhood nutritional deficiencies stunting bone growth

explanation: Poor nutrition during a girl's growing years can stunt bone development, affecting the full growth of her bony pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h1)

question: Which part of the female pelvis forms the actual bony passage that the baby travels through during birth?
explanation: The true pelvis sits below the pelvic brim and contains the inlet, cavity, and outlet that the baby must pass through. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which landmark forms the back boundary of the pelvic inlet?
explanation: The sacral promontory juts forward at the back of the pelvis to mark the prominent rear boundary of the pelvic inlet. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which imaging method is avoided during pregnancy due to the risk of radiation to the baby?
explanation: X-ray pelvimetry uses ionizing radiation which can harm a growing fetus, so clinical physical exams are preferred instead. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the primary method used by midwives to assess internal pelvic dimensions during antenatal care?
explanation: Midwives use sterile gloved fingers during a clinical vaginal examination to manually evaluate the internal spaces and landmarks of the pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h3)

question: Around how many weeks of pregnancy is a clinical pelvic assessment usually done if performed during antenatal care?
explanation: This check is usually done late in the third trimester when pelvic tissues are softer, or when the mother is admitted in early labor. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h4)

question: When a midwife checks the subpubic angle during an exam, what is commonly used to estimate the angle?

options.A: The entire examining hand spread wide
options.D: Two examining fingers placed side by side

explanation: Placing two examining fingers beneath the pubic arch helps the midwife feel if the angle is wide enough. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h4)

question: What does it mean if a midwife can easily reach the sacral promontory during a vaginal examination?
explanation: If the sacral promontory is easily reached with the fingers, it indicates a short diagonal conjugate, which points to an inlet contraction. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which finding strongly suggests a mid-pelvic narrowing that could slow down or block the baby's descent?

options.A: A high and unreachable sacral promontory
options.B: A wide and open subpubic angle

explanation: Prominent ischial spines narrow the space in the mid-pelvis, leaving less room for the baby to turn and move down. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the best action when a midwife finds a clear pelvic contraction during antenatal care?

options.A: Refer the patient for facility delivery with surgical capabilities
options.B: Prescribe muscle relaxants to widen the pelvic bones
options.C: Encourage prolonged active labor exercises at home
options.D: Advise the woman to plan for a home birth with a traditional birth attendant

explanation: A contracted pelvis requires giving birth in a center where a Caesarean section can be safely done if labor gets blocked. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why is it important to plan early for transport and emergency funds when a woman has a contracted pelvis?

options.A: To pay for mandatory X-ray pelvimetry at 38 weeks
options.B: To prevent dangerous delays in reaching a surgical center during labor
options.C: To cover the high cost of routine home delivery kits
options.D: To purchase herbal concoctions that soften pelvic ligaments

explanation: Setting up transport ahead of time ensures the mother gets to a referral hospital quickly when labor starts, avoiding serious complications. [learn more](BMP210_U1_T8#BMP210_U1_T8_h6)

question: What anatomical structure forms the anterior boundary of the vulva?
explanation: The mons pubis sits over the pubic bone at the front, marking the upper or anterior limit of the vulva. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h1)

question: During a normal delivery, a midwife checks a tear near the back part of the vulva. Which structure is most likely involved?
explanation: The perineal body forms the posterior boundary of the vulva and is the most common site for tears during childbirth. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which skin folds lie directly inside the labia majora and enclose the vestibule?
explanation: The labia minora are the inner folds of skin that frame the vestibule and protect the vaginal and urethral openings. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h2)

question: What happens when Bartholin's glands become infected or blocked?

options.A: They regulate the structural support of the pubic symphysis
options.B: They produce excessive pubic hair during pregnancy
options.C: They reside in the vestibule and can form painful cysts or abscesses
options.D: They directly control the hormonal cycle of menstruation

explanation: The ducts of Bartholin's glands open into the vestibule, and blockage of these ducts leads to painful fluid accumulation and infection. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which main blood vessel is the primary source of arterial blood to the vulva?
explanation: The internal pudendal artery supplies most of the blood to the external genitalia. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h3)

question: Why does a superficial tear on the vulva during delivery often swell up very quickly?

options.A: Lymphatic vessels dilate rapidly to absorb amniotic fluid
options.B: Arterial pressure in the pelvis drops sharply during the second stage
options.C: Skeletal muscles in the perineum contract continuously
options.D: The vulva contains a dense network of blood vessels and erectile tissue

explanation: The rich vascular network and erectile tissue in the vulva lead to fast bleeding and hematoma formation when injured. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h3)

question: Where does the majority of lymphatic fluid from the vulva drain to first?
explanation: The superficial inguinal nodes in the groin are the primary destination for vulvar lymph drainage. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h4)

question: A patient has an infected wound on the labia majora. Which lymph nodes should the midwife check first?
explanation: Because the labia majora drain directly to the superficial inguinal nodes, infection in this area commonly causes groin node enlargement. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which nerve provides the main sensation and movement to the perineum?
explanation: The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) is the primary nerve supplying the perineal structures. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why is a pudendal nerve block helpful for pain relief during an instrumental vaginal delivery?

options.A: It blocks parasympathetic impulses to the urinary bladder
options.B: It relaxes the smooth muscle fibres inside the uterine body
options.C: It numbs the somatic sensory fibers supplying the lower vagina and perineum
options.D: It stops sympathetic vasoconstriction in the femoral vessels

explanation: Blocking the pudendal nerve desensitizes the perineal tissues, providing excellent pain relief for repairs and instrumental births. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h5)

question: What causes the bluish discoloration of the vulva and vagina observed during early pregnancy?

options.A: Chronic inflammation of the Bartholin's ducts
options.C: Melanin deposition from rising estrogen levels
options.D: Decreased cardiac output to the lower extremities

explanation: The extra blood flow and congestion in pregnancy create a bluish hue known as Chadwick's sign. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h6)

question: A postpartum woman has severe, throbbing perineal pain a few hours after a normal delivery, even though her stitches are intact. What condition should the midwife suspect?
explanation: Severe, disproportionate perineal pain with swelling often indicates hidden bleeding into the tissues, forming a hematoma. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T1#BMP210_U2_T1_h6)

question: Which of the following structures is housed entirely within the true pelvis alongside the uterus and ovaries?
explanation: The fallopian tubes, along with the uterus, ovaries, and cervix, are internal reproductive organs located inside the true pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is it clinically useful for midwives to know the supportive ligaments and structures of the internal genitalia?

options.A: To determine the total bone density of the maternal pelvis
options.B: To measure hormone levels directly from the pelvic floor muscles
options.C: To understand how organs stay anchored and stretch during pregnancy
options.D: To calculate the exact date of ovulation every single month

explanation: Ligaments and pelvic floor muscles provide structural support while accommodating the massive expansion needed during gestation. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h1)

question: Name the thick middle layer of the uterine wall made of smooth muscle.
explanation: The myometrium forms the muscular bulk of the uterus and drives contractions during childbirth. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which part of the uterus represents the rounded upper portion situated above the insertion of the fallopian tubes?
explanation: The fundus is the dome-shaped top of the uterus that midwives palpate during abdominal exams to assess postpartum involution. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the name of the lower opening of the cervix that faces directly into the vagina?
explanation: The external os is the vaginal opening of the cervix, which dilates significantly during the first stage of labor. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h3)

question: How does progesterone affect cervical mucus after ovulation has occurred?

options.A: It makes the mucus thick and sticky to block sperm and germs
options.B: It turns the mucus into an acidic fluid that destroys the ovum
options.C: It makes the mucus clear and stretchy to help sperm swim fast
options.D: It stops all mucus production completely across the cervix

explanation: Progesterone dominates the luteal phase, creating a dense barrier in the cervical canal to protect the uterine environment. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h3)

question: In which specific segment of the fallopian tube does fertilization of the ovum usually happen?
explanation: The wide ampulla provides the optimal environment and space for the sperm to meet and fertilize the secondary oocyte. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h4)

question: What do we call the finger-like projections at the end of the fallopian tube that sweep over the ovary?
explanation: Fimbriae catch the released egg during ovulation and guide it gently into the opening of the fallopian tube. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which temporary endocrine structure does a ruptured ovarian follicle turn into after ovulation?
explanation: The corpus luteum forms from the leftover follicular cells and pumps out progesterone to support a potential pregnancy. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why are the ovaries considered both exocrine and endocrine organs?

options.A: They produce digestive enzymes alongside monthly menstrual blood flow
options.B: They filter waste products from the pelvis while storing urine temporarily
options.C: They control both voluntary leg movements and involuntary uterine contractions
options.D: They release egg cells and also secrete reproductive hormones into the bloodstream

explanation: Ovaries produce gametes (ova) and secrete key hormones like estrogen and progesterone directly into the blood supply. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which major blood vessel is the direct origin of the ovarian artery in the female pelvis?
explanation: Unlike the uterine artery which branches from the internal iliac, the ovarian artery arises directly from the abdominal aorta high in the abdomen. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h6)

question: Where does the lymphatic fluid from the ovaries primarily drain to?
explanation: Because ovaries originate high in the posterior abdominal wall during embryonic development, their lymphatic drainage travels up to the lumbar and aortic nodes. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h6)

question: Why must surgeons exercise extreme caution around the uterine artery during pelvic surgeries like a cesarean section?

options.A: It connects directly to the maternal heart via the subclavian vein
options.B: It runs in close proximity to the ureter as it approaches the uterus
options.C: It houses the main nerve bundle controlling bladder sensation
options.D: It supplies the entire blood volume to the lower extremities

explanation: The close anatomical relationship between the uterine artery and the ureter puts the urinary tract at risk during pelvic vessel ligation. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h7)

question: In which part of the reproductive tract do the vast majority of ectopic pregnancies implant and grow?
explanation: The wide ampulla is the most common site where a fertilized ovum implants abnormally instead of reaching the uterine cavity. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T2#BMP210_U2_T2_h7)

question: Which muscular layer of the uterus contracts strongly during labor?
explanation: The myometrium is the thick middle layer made of smooth muscle that generates the powerful contractions needed to push the baby out during labor. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why does only part of the endometrium shed during menstruation?

options.A: The perimetrium protects the deep glands from damage.
options.B: The cervical canal blocks the upper layer from escaping.
options.C: The basal layer remains behind to rebuild the functional layer.
options.D: The myometrium absorbs the remaining tissue to nourish the body.

explanation: The endometrium is split into two zones where the superficial functional layer sheds, but the deep basal layer stays intact to regenerate it for the next cycle. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the name of the dome-shaped upper part of the uterus above the fallopian tubes?
explanation: The fundus is the rounded top portion of the uterus located above where the fallopian tubes enter. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h2)

question: A midwife assesses a pregnant woman in labor and notes that the lower uterine segment has thinned out. Which anatomical landmark formed this segment?
explanation: The short narrow region called the isthmus stretches and thins remarkably during late pregnancy and labor to create the lower uterine segment. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which ligaments provide the primary mechanical support that prevents the uterus from dropping or prolapsing?
explanation: The cardinal ligaments extend from the cervix to the pelvic walls and carry the main weight-bearing load to keep the uterus from descending into the vagina. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h3)

question: Where do the round ligaments eventually terminate after leaving the uterine horns?
explanation: Round ligaments travel through the inguinal canal and insert into the soft tissue of the labia majora in the external genitalia. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary vessel supplying oxygenated blood to the uterus?
explanation: The uterine artery branches off the internal iliac artery and serves as the main blood conduit feeding the uterus. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why is the close crossing of the uterine artery and the ureter important during pelvic surgery?

options.A: The artery runs inside the ureter lumen throughout its entire pelvic course.
options.B: The artery blocks urine flow if the patient drinks too much water before surgery.
options.C: The ureter can be accidentally ligated or cut because it lies directly beneath the artery.
options.D: The ureter supplies extra blood to the uterine artery during stressful procedures.

explanation: Surgeons must be extremely careful near the cervix because the uterine artery crosses directly over the ureter, risking accidental damage. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h4)

question: Where does the lymphatic fluid from the uterine fundus primarily drain?
explanation: Lymphatics from the upper fundus travel upward with the ovarian vessels to drain into the lumbar or aortic lymph nodes. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which pelvic structure drains lymphatic fluid directly into the internal and external iliac nodes?
explanation: The lower uterine body and the cervix route their lymphatic drainage primarily into the internal and external iliac node chains in the pelvis. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T3#BMP210_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which gland releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone into the body?
explanation: The hypothalamus is the specialized brain structure responsible for pulsing out gonadotropin-releasing hormone to direct the pituitary gland. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h1)

question: During most of the menstrual cycle, how do ovarian hormones affect the hypothalamus and pituitary gland?
explanation: For the majority of the cycle, circulating estrogen and progesterone suppress the hypothalamus and pituitary to keep hormone levels balanced. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h1)

question: What kind of cells surround the egg cell in a resting, primordial follicle?

options.B: A single layer of flattened squamous cells
options.C: A dense layer of mucus and cilia

explanation: Primordial follicles feature a resting egg cell enclosed simply by a single layer of flat, squamous cells. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h2)

question: What is the medical term for the natural breakdown of ovarian follicles before they reach maturity?
explanation: Atresia is the natural process where the vast majority of developing follicles break down and are absorbed by the ovary rather than ovulating. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which specific cell layer in a developing follicle responds to luteinizing hormone by making androgens?
explanation: Theca interna cells have receptors for luteinizing hormone, which stimulates them to produce androgens that are later converted to estrogen. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h3)

question: Why does usually only a single dominant follicle survive to maturity during a normal cycle?

options.A: It physically blocks blood supply to all other neighboring follicles.
options.B: It secretes toxins that destroy every other follicle in both ovaries.
options.C: It absorbs all the calcium present in the surrounding ovarian stroma.
options.D: It develops more FSH receptors and survives despite falling FSH levels.

explanation: The dominant follicle outcompetes the others by building up more FSH receptors, allowing it to thrive even when overall hormone levels drop. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h3)

question: What hormonal event directly triggers the rupture of the mature follicle during ovulation?

options.A: A sustained spike in inhibin levels
options.C: A sudden drop in basal progesterone
options.D: A sharp decrease in circulating estrogen

explanation: The mid-cycle LH surge is the master trigger that weakens the ovarian wall and prompts the release of the oocyte. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is the main job of prostaglandins produced inside the follicle right before ovulation?

options.A: To prevent the egg cell from undergoing premature cell division
options.B: To weaken and digest the wall of the ovary at the stigma
options.C: To stop the production of progesterone by the theca cells
options.D: To attract sperm cells into the peritoneal cavity early

explanation: Prostaglandins cause localized tissue changes, thinning the ovarian surface so the egg can escape easily. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h4)

question: What primary hormone is produced in large amounts by a healthy corpus luteum?
explanation: The corpus luteum specializes in making progesterone, which prepares and stabilizes the uterine lining for a potential pregnancy. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h5)

question: What chemical signal prevents the corpus luteum from breaking down if an embryo successfully implants?
explanation: The early placenta secretes human chorionic gonadotropin, which signals the corpus luteum to keep producing progesterone and maintain the pregnancy. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h5)

question: A client trying to conceive asks why her basal body temperature rises slightly in the second half of her cycle. What physiological explanation should the midwife give?

options.A: The developing placenta releases adrenaline to increase maternal energy.
options.B: Metabolic activity inside the maturing oocyte generates excess body heat.
options.C: Estrogen surge right before ovulation causes a temporary fever.
options.D: Progesterone released by the corpus luteum raises core body temperature.

explanation: Progesterone has a thermogenic effect on the hypothalamus, causing a measurable rise in basal body temperature following ovulation. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which condition involves the halt of multiple ovarian follicles before a dominant one can form?
explanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome involves hormonal imbalances that stop normal follicle development, leaving many small arrested follicles in the ovaries. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T4#BMP210_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary physiological purpose of the endometrial cycle?

options.A: To stimulate mature egg release from the ovaries
options.B: To prepare the uterus for potential embryo implantation
options.C: To regulate daily basal body temperature changes
options.D: To maintain normal pelvic floor muscle tone

explanation: The monthly changes in the endometrial lining are specifically designed to create a fertile, receptive environment where a fertilized egg can successfully implant and grow. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which two primary hormones directly drive the cyclic changes in the endometrial lining?
explanation: Ovarian hormones, specifically estrogen and progesterone, act directly on the uterine tissue to orchestrate the phases of the endometrial cycle. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which layer of the endometrium is completely shed during menstruation?
explanation: The superficial stratum functionalis breaks down and sloughs off every month when hormone levels drop, while the deeper layer stays behind. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h2)

question: Why is the stratum basalis so important for the endometrial cycle?

options.A: It acts as the permanent foundation that regenerates the shed functional layer.
options.B: It produces all the progesterone needed for early pregnancy.
options.C: It stores the unfertilized eggs before they reach the uterine cavity.
options.D: It forms the muscular wall that contracts during menstrual cramps.

explanation: Because the stratum basalis survives menstruation, its cells rapidly multiply to rebuild a brand-new functional layer for the next cycle. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h2)

question: What triggers the onset of the menstrual phase?

options.A: A sharp drop in estrogen and progesterone levels
options.B: Complete closure of the internal cervical os
options.C: A sudden surge in luteinizing hormone release
options.D: The initial rapid growth of the ovarian follicles

explanation: When hormone levels fall rapidly due to the breakdown of the corpus luteum, the uterine lining loses its hormonal support and begins to shed. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why do the spiral arteries clamp down tightly right before menstruation starts?

options.A: Myometrial contractions squeeze the blood vessels shut to prevent excessive bleeding.
options.B: An implanting embryo sends chemical signals that shut down local circulation.
options.C: Sudden hormone withdrawal restricts blood flow to the lining, causing it to shed.
options.D: High levels of estrogen force the vessels to expand rapidly until they burst.

explanation: The drop in progesterone causes the spiral arteries to constrict, starving the upper endometrial layers of oxygen and causing them to break away. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h3)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for driving the proliferative phase of the endometrium?
explanation: Estrogen stimulates the rapid growth and repair of the uterine lining after menstruation has finished. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h4)

question: What happens inside the uterus during the proliferative phase?

options.A: The endometrial lining rebuilds and thickens under hormonal stimulation.
options.B: Blood vessels clamp shut to prepare for tissue damage.
options.C: Superficial tissue dies and sloughs off through the vagina.
options.D: Uterine muscles contract rhythmically to expel fluid.

explanation: Cells from the basalis layer divide and multiply to create a fresh, thick functional layer in preparation for a possible pregnancy. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which ovarian hormone dominates and characterizes the secretory phase?
explanation: Progesterone takes over after ovulation to transform the thick uterine lining into a secretory, nutrient-rich environment. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h5)

question: A client has a defective corpus luteum that produces very little progesterone. Which phase of her cycle will be directly affected?
explanation: Because progesterone is the primary driver of the secretory phase, low levels prevent the proper glandular maturation and secretion needed for implantation. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why does a cycle without ovulation often cause irregular and heavy bleeding?

options.A: Spiral arteries undergo permanent spasm, preventing normal tissue healing after menses.
options.B: The endometrium thickens continuously under estrogen without progesterone to stabilize it, leading to unpredictable shedding.
options.C: The corpus luteum produces excessive progesterone that destroys the stratum basalis layer.
options.D: The pituitary gland secretes large amounts of oxytocin, causing continuous contractions.

explanation: Without ovulation, progesterone is absent, so the lining grows haphazardly until it outgrows its blood supply and sheds irregularly. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding in women of reproductive age?

options.A: Benign structural growths like uterine fibroids
options.B: Complete absence of the anterior pituitary gland
options.C: Hormonal imbalances from cycles without ovulation

explanation: While pituitary dysfunction can affect cycles, a complete absence of the anterior pituitary is an extremely rare congenital condition, whereas common causes include anovulation and fibroids. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T5#BMP210_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which body system uses chemical messengers (hormones) sent through the bloodstream to cause slow, long-lasting changes?
explanation: Hormones are released by endocrine glands and travel through the blood to target organs. This creates a slower, longer-lasting response compared to fast nerve impulses. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why do endocrine signals take longer to work than nerve signals?

options.A: Hormones must travel through the bloodstream to reach target tissues
options.B: Endocrine glands store very little chemical substance
options.C: Target cells actively block incoming hormones at first
options.D: Nerve impulses move slower than liquid blood flow

explanation: Circulation time determines how long it takes for a hormone to reach its specific receptor site, making the response more gradual than electrical nerve signals. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which part of the brain is the main link between the nervous system and the endocrine system?
explanation: The hypothalamus receives signals from various parts of the brain and releases hormones that control the pituitary gland. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h2)

question: A blockage in which specific blood vessel network would immediately stop hypothalamic hormones from reaching the anterior pituitary?
explanation: The hypophysial portal system carries blood directly from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary, ensuring high hormone concentrations reach the target cells. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h2)

question: How must Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) be released from the hypothalamus to keep the pituitary working normally?

options.A: In response to high uterine pressure

explanation: Pulsatile secretion prevents receptor downregulation, which happens when pituitary cells are exposed to constant, uninterrupted hormone levels. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h3)

question: What happens to pituitary hormone production if a patient receives continuous, non-stop synthetic GnRH for a long time?

options.A: It shifts to producing only prolactin
options.B: It accelerates the onset of ovulation
options.C: It increases to dangerously high levels
options.D: It becomes suppressed or shut down

explanation: Constant exposure desensitizes the pituitary receptors, causing a drop in FSH and LH release, which is used therapeutically to suppress sex hormone production. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which anterior pituitary hormone is mainly responsible for triggering ovulation mid-cycle?
explanation: A sharp, massive surge of LH from the anterior pituitary directly causes the mature follicle to rupture and release the egg. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the main job of FSH during the first half of the menstrual cycle (the follicular phase)?

options.A: Maintaining the endometrial lining after implantation
options.B: Stopping all estrogen production in the ovaries
options.C: Causing immediate degeneration of the corpus luteum
options.D: Promoting the growth and recruitment of ovarian follicles

explanation: FSH stimulates a group of ovarian follicles to grow, helping select the dominant follicle that will move on to ovulation. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h4)

question: Which hormone is produced in large amounts by the corpus luteum after ovulation to prepare the uterine lining?
explanation: The corpus luteum secretes abundant progesterone, which changes the uterine lining into a secretory, nutrient-rich bed ready for a fertilized egg. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why do theca cells and granulosa cells need to work together to make estrogen?

options.A: Granulosa cells cannot survive without direct physical touch from theca cells
options.B: Theca cells make androgens that granulosa cells must convert into estrogen
options.C: Theca cells block FSH from entering the ovarian tissue
options.D: Granulosa cells produce all the necessary cholesterol without outside help

explanation: Neither cell type alone has all the enzymes needed to make estrogen from scratch. Theca cells make the starting androgens, and granulosa cells convert them into estrogen. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h5)

question: What triggers the mid-cycle LH surge through positive feedback?

options.A: Complete absence of gonadotropins in the blood
options.B: Sustained high levels of estrogen from the mature follicle
options.C: A sudden drop in core body temperature
options.D: High levels of progesterone secreted by immature follicles

explanation: Unlike the rest of the cycle where estrogen suppresses hormone release, peak estrogen levels paradoxically trigger a burst of GnRH and LH. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a function of negative feedback during the normal menstrual cycle?

options.A: Causing the mid-cycle LH surge that forces ovulation
options.B: Preventing the development of new follicles while the corpus luteum is active
options.C: Suppressing excessive FSH release during the luteal phase
options.D: Keeping baseline gonadotropin levels low in the early follicular phase

explanation: The mid-cycle surge is driven by positive feedback. Negative feedback is used to suppress and control hormone levels at other times in the cycle. [learn more](BMP210_U2_T6#BMP210_U2_T6_h6)

question: When do midwives usually perform the first check of a newborn boy's external genitalia?

options.C: At six weeks of postnatal life
options.D: Only if the mother requests it

explanation: Midwives perform a newborn physical check shortly after birth to confirm normal development and catch any issues early. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why do midwifery students learn the anatomy of the male external genitalia?

options.B: To perform surgical corrections in the labor ward
options.C: To prescribe hormonal treatments for newborns
options.D: To accurately identify normal structures and spot congenital abnormalities

explanation: Knowing normal anatomy helps midwives recognize variations, reassure parents, and make timely referrals when needed. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the name of the tough fibrous layer that encloses the erectile tissue inside the penis?
explanation: The tunica albuginea is a strong fibrous sheath that wraps around the erectile tissue columns within the penile shaft. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which specific structure contains the spongy urethra inside the shaft of the penis?
explanation: The corpus spongiosum runs along the underside of the penis and surrounds the urethra as it travels toward the tip. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which part of the nervous system triggers the relaxation of penile blood vessels to produce an erection?
explanation: Parasympathetic nerve signals cause blood vessels in the erectile tissue to widen, allowing blood to fill the chambers. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the term for the process where rhythmic muscle contractions in the pelvis expel semen?
explanation: Ejaculation is the expulsion of semen driven by coordinated muscular contractions in the pelvic region. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h3)

question: Why does the scrotum keep the testes at a slightly lower temperature than core body heat?
explanation: Normal sperm development requires a cooler environment than the internal body temperature provides. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h4)

question: What does the cremaster muscle do when the body is exposed to a cold environment?

options.A: It relaxes to let the testes hang lower
options.B: It pulls the testes closer to the body wall
options.C: It closes the inguinal canal completely
options.D: It flattens the scrotal skin to release sweat

explanation: The cremaster muscle reflexively contracts in response to cold to keep the testes warm near the pelvic cavity. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the name of the fibrous cord that guides the testes downward during fetal development?
explanation: The gubernaculum acts as a guide, pulling the testis from the abdomen down through the canal and into the scrotum. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h5)

question: A preterm baby boy is born at 32 weeks, and his scrotal sacs feel empty and cannot be felt. What is the best initial action for the midwife?

options.A: Document the finding and monitor during routine postnatal visits
options.B: Perform an immediate surgical repositioning procedure
options.D: Tell the mother the condition is permanent and untreatable

explanation: Many preterm infants experience delayed descent that corrects itself over the first few months, so monitoring is the appropriate step. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h5)

question: Where is the opening of the urethra located in a newborn with hypospadias?

options.A: On the dorsal top surface of the penis
options.B: Inside the perineal raphe behind the scrotum
options.C: On the ventral underside of the penis
options.D: Directly at the center of the glans tip

explanation: Hypospadias happens when the urethral tube does not close all the way to the tip, leaving the opening on the underside. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h6)

question: What physical sign helps a midwife tell a simple hydrocele apart from other scrotal swellings?

options.A: It transilluminates brightly when a light source is applied
options.B: It causes severe acute pain in the neonate
options.C: It feels hard and bony upon palpation
options.D: It disappears completely when the infant cries

explanation: Because a hydrocele is filled with clear fluid, light passes through it easily, lighting up the scrotum during transillumination. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why is it important to examine a newborn boy in a warm room?

options.A: To keep the vernix caseosa from drying out too quickly
options.B: To prevent the cremasteric reflex from pulling the testes upward
options.C: To stop the infant from crying during the examination
options.D: To ensure the urethral meatus dilates fully

explanation: Cold air triggers the cremaster muscle to contract, pulling the testes up and making them hard to feel during the check. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT part of a standard newborn genital check for a male infant?

options.A: Measuring the exact length of the vas deferens
options.B: Palpating both halves of the scrotal sac
options.C: Checking the position of the urethral meatus
options.D: Inspecting the penis for abnormal curvature or swelling

explanation: The vas deferens is an internal duct deep inside the spermatic cord and cannot be measured during a routine external newborn exam. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T1#BMP210_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is the main cell type produced by the internal male reproductive organs?
explanation: The male reproductive system is designed to produce male gametes, which are known as spermatozoa. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is knowing about male reproductive anatomy useful for midwives?

options.A: It is required for diagnosing prostate cancer in labor wards.
options.B: It helps with family health counseling and fertility care.
options.C: It allows midwives to perform surgical vasectomies safely.
options.D: It directly guides the management of third-stage postpartum hemorrhage.

explanation: Midwives frequently counsel couples on family planning, making a good grasp of both male and female anatomy very helpful. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which specific cells inside the testes make testosterone?
explanation: The Leydig cells are found in the tissue between the seminiferous tubules and are responsible for secreting testosterone. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h2)

question: Where does sperm production actually take place inside the testes?
explanation: Sperm cells are continuously made inside the tiny, coiled networks called the seminiferous tubules. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is the main job of the epididymis?
explanation: Sperm enter the epididymis immature and gain the ability to swim and mature while they are stored there. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h3)

question: What would happen to sperm if they left the seminiferous tubules without passing through the epididymis?

options.A: They would transform into endocrine-producing cells instead.
options.B: They would lack forward motility and fertilization capacity.
options.C: They would instantly dissolve due to acidic pH levels.
options.D: They would immediately multiply into millions of new cells.

explanation: Passing through the epididymis gives sperm the ability to move properly and fertilize an egg. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which muscular tube carries sperm out of the scrotum and into the pelvic cavity?
explanation: The vas deferens serves as the main tube transporting sperm upward from the scrotum into the pelvic cavity. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h4)

question: During a vasectomy, a surgeon cuts a tube in the spermatic cord. Which tube is this?
explanation: A vasectomy involves cutting and sealing the vas deferens to stop sperm from entering the ejaculate. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h4)

question: Which two structures join together to form each ejaculatory duct?

options.D: Vas deferens and seminal vesicle duct

explanation: The duct from the seminal vesicle merges with the vas deferens to create the ejaculatory duct. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h5)

question: Where do the ejaculatory ducts empty their contents during ejaculation?
explanation: The ejaculatory ducts run through the prostate gland and open directly into the prostatic section of the urethra. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is a common cause of blockages in the sperm transport tubes that can lead to male infertility?

options.D: Excessive exposure to cold scrotal air

explanation: Infections can lead to scarring and blockages within the delicate tubes of the epididymis and vas deferens. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which of these conditions is NOT related to the male reproductive system?
explanation: Uterine fibroids grow in the female muscular wall of the uterus and have nothing to do with male anatomy. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T2#BMP210_U3_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary function of the male accessory glands?

options.D: Producing the liquid portion of semen

explanation: The testes make sperm, but the accessory glands provide the fluids that mix with sperm to form semen. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why does sperm need the secretions produced by the accessory glands?

options.A: To prevent the sperm from swimming too fast
options.B: To help the testes produce more testosterone
options.C: To survive the acidic environment of the female tract
options.D: To help the body filter waste products

explanation: The female reproductive tract is acidic, and gland secretions help protect and nourish sperm so they can survive. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h1)

question: Where are the seminal vesicles located in the male body?

options.B: At the base of the penis

explanation: The seminal vesicles sit posterior to the urinary bladder near the base of the bladder. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of fructose found in seminal vesicle fluid?

options.C: Lowering the acidity of the vagina
options.D: Killing harmful bacteria in the tract

explanation: Sperm require a lot of energy to swim, and the fructose in the seminal fluid acts as a fuel source. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h2)

question: Which of the following describes the location of the prostate gland?

options.A: Inside the walls of the testicles
options.B: At the very tip of the penis

explanation: The prostate sits right under the bladder and surrounds the urethra. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h3)

question: What urinary symptom is most likely to happen when a man has an enlarged prostate gland?

options.A: Difficulty passing urine because the urethra is squeezed
options.B: Painful contractions in the scrotal sac
options.C: Complete inability to produce any seminal fluid
options.D: A sudden increase in testosterone levels

explanation: Since the urethra passes directly through the prostate, an enlarged prostate squeezes the tube and blocks urine flow. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h3)

question: What is another common name for the bulbourethral glands?
explanation: The bulbourethral glands are frequently called Cowper's glands in anatomical texts. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h4)

question: Why do the bulbourethral glands secrete fluid before ejaculation occurs?

options.A: To provide energy for the swimming sperm
options.C: To clear and neutralize acid in the urethra
options.D: To manufacture the majority of the semen

explanation: Urine leaves traces of acid in the urethra, so the bulbourethral secretion neutralizes this acid before sperm travel through. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which gland contributes the largest percentage of fluid to total semen volume?
explanation: The seminal vesicles provide the bulk of the seminal fluid, making up about 60 to 70 percent of the total volume. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h5)

question: How do the secretions of the prostate and bulbourethral glands work together regarding acidity?

options.A: One creates acid while the other creates a base
options.B: They remove all acid from the male reproductive tract
options.C: Both secrete alkaline substances to neutralize acids
options.D: They make the semen acidic to match the vagina

explanation: Both the prostate and bulbourethral glands provide alkaline fluids that neutralize harmful acids found in the urethra and vagina. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h5)

question: What does the term benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) mean?

options.A: Complete blockage of the seminal vesicles
options.C: Severe bacterial infection of the testicles

explanation: Benign means non-cancerous, and prostatic hyperplasia refers to the growth and enlargement of the prostate gland. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h6)

question: Why can an infection in the accessory glands lead to male infertility?

options.A: It changes the fluid balance and harms sperm movement
options.B: It stops the testes from producing any testosterone
options.C: It causes the penis to become completely flaccid
options.D: It permanently closes the muscular vas deferens

explanation: Infections alter the normal chemical composition of seminal fluid, making it difficult for sperm to survive or swim properly. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T3#BMP210_U3_T3_h6)

question: Where does spermatogenesis take place inside the male reproductive system?
explanation: Sperm production happens specifically inside the tiny, coiled tubes located within the testes called the seminiferous tubules. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h1)

question: What is a major difference between male spermatogenesis and female oogenesis?

options.B: Oogenesis occurs inside the seminiferous tubules

explanation: While a woman is born with all her eggs, a man's testes continuously produce new sperm from puberty until old age. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h1)

question: Which specific cell type undergoes the first meiotic division during sperm production?
explanation: Primary spermatocytes are the diploid cells that enter the first meiotic division to halve the chromosome number. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h2)

question: What is the main physical change that happens during spermiogenesis?

options.A: Mature sperm gain the ability to swim in the epididymis
options.B: Round spermatids transform into streamlined spermatozoa
options.C: Secondary spermatocytes complete the first meiotic split
options.D: Diploid spermatogonia multiply rapidly through mitosis

explanation: Spermiogenesis is the physical remodeling phase where a round, simple cell develops a tail, a middle piece, and an acrosome head. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which cells in the testes respond to luteinizing hormone by producing testosterone?
explanation: Leydig cells sit outside the tubules and produce testosterone when signaled by luteinizing hormone from the pituitary. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary role of inhibin during male hormonal control?

options.A: Helping sperm swim faster inside the female reproductive tract
options.B: Providing negative feedback to slow down FSH release
options.C: Directly forcing Leydig cells to manufacture testosterone
options.D: Stimulating the hypothalamus to release more GnRH

explanation: Inhibin is released by Sertoli cells to signal the pituitary gland to reduce follicle-stimulating hormone when sperm production is sufficient. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary function of the acrosome located on the sperm head?

options.A: Releasing enzymes to break through the outer layers of the egg
options.B: Producing testosterone to signal nearby supporting cells
options.C: Generating chemical energy to power the movement of the tail
options.D: Protecting the haploid nucleus from damage in the vagina

explanation: The acrosome contains powerful digestive enzymes that break down the protective barriers surrounding the ovum during fertilization. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h4)

question: A laboratory analysis shows a sample of sperm has structural defects entirely restricted to the midpiece. What specific function is most likely impaired?

options.A: Penetration of the egg's outer shell
options.B: Binding to the wall of the fallopian tube
options.D: Carrying the correct haploid DNA count

explanation: The midpiece contains mitochondria, which are the powerhouses that generate the energy required for flagellar movement. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which accessory gland contributes the largest volume of fluid to human semen?
explanation: The seminal vesicles provide roughly 60 to 70 percent of total semen volume, including fructose to feed the sperm. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why do bulbourethral glands secrete mucus just prior to ejaculation?

options.A: To stimulate the pituitary gland to release more LH
options.B: To provide extra fructose energy for active sperm
options.C: To neutralize acidic traces of urine in the urethra
options.D: To form a hard protective plug inside the vagina

explanation: The clear mucus secreted by Cowper's glands cleanses and neutralizes the urethra so the passing sperm are not damaged by acid. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h5)

question: What medical term describes an absolute absence of spermatozoa in a semen sample?
explanation: Azoospermia refers to the complete lack of sperm cells in the ejaculate, whereas oligospermia refers to a low count. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h6)

question: Why can a severe fever experienced today take over two months to affect a man's sperm count?

options.A: The hypothalamus delays sending inhibitory signals to the pituitary gland
options.B: The full cycle of spermatogenesis takes approximately 64 to 74 days
options.C: Testosterone levels take months to drop after a mild viral infection
options.D: Sperm stored in the prostate gland remain viable for several months

explanation: Because it takes over two months for a germ cell to mature into an ejaculated spermatozoon, insults to the testes take that long to appear in semen analysis. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T4#BMP210_U3_T4_h6)

question: How does the male reproductive endocrine system generally function compared to the female system?
explanation: Male hormone production remains relatively steady day to day, unlike the cyclic monthly fluctuations of the female reproductive system. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h1)

question: Name the primary bodily system responsible for coordinating male reproductive hormones.
explanation: The endocrine system uses chemical messengers called hormones to regulate bodily functions, including reproduction. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which specific brain structure releases Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)?
explanation: Specialized neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus produce and release GnRH into a local portal system leading to the pituitary gland. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h2)

question: What is the primary function of the anterior pituitary gland within the HPT axis?

options.A: Producing GnRH to stimulate the hypothalamus
options.B: Directly producing high levels of testosterone
options.C: Storing mature sperm cells before ejaculation
options.D: Releasing LH and FSH in response to GnRH

explanation: The anterior pituitary acts as the middle manager of the axis, taking signals from the hypothalamus and releasing gonadotropins to the testes. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h2)

question: Which cells inside the testes are stimulated directly by Luteinizing Hormone (LH)?
explanation: LH binds to receptors on the Leydig cells in the interstitial space, signaling them to manufacture testosterone. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary target cell for Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) in the male testes?
explanation: FSH supports sperm production by directly stimulating the Sertoli nurse cells within the seminiferous tubules. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h3)

question: Which precursor molecule do the Leydig cells primarily use to synthesize testosterone?
explanation: Cholesterol serves as the foundational raw material for creating steroid hormones, including testosterone. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why is the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase important in male hormone action?

options.A: It transports testosterone safely through the bloodstream
options.B: It converts testosterone into the stronger androgen DHT
options.C: It helps the pituitary gland manufacture more LH
options.D: It breaks down excess testosterone to stop puberty early

explanation: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is a potent derivative of testosterone responsible for many specific male secondary sex characteristics. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h4)

question: What happens to the release of GnRH and LH when blood testosterone levels become very high?

options.A: Their production stops completely and permanently
options.B: Their release is suppressed by negative feedback
options.C: Their chemical structure changes to match DHT
options.D: Their release increases to speed up production

explanation: High levels of testosterone signal the brain and pituitary to slow down hormonal output, keeping levels balanced. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h5)

question: Which specific substance do Sertoli cells release to selectively inhibit the secretion of FSH?
explanation: Inhibin acts as a feedback signal from the testes to the anterior pituitary, telling it to dial back FSH release. [learn more](BMP210_U3_T5#BMP210_U3_T5_h5)

question: How many chromosomes are in a normal human cell made by meiosis?
explanation: Meiosis cuts the chromosome number in half, changing the standard 46 chromosomes down to 23 in each mature sex cell. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is the main benefit of crossing over during meiosis?

options.A: It stops cells from dividing too early
options.B: It speeds up cell division in the reproductive organs
options.C: It mixes up genes to create unique traits in offspring
options.D: It doubles the total number of chromosomes

explanation: During crossing over, sections of DNA swap between chromosome pairs, ensuring each sperm and egg carries a different mix of traits. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h1)

question: When do human females start forming their primary oocytes?

options.A: At the start of the first menstrual period
options.B: During fetal development in the womb
options.C: Only after a sperm enters the egg

explanation: A baby girl forms all her primary oocytes while growing inside her mother's uterus, long before she is born. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h2)

question: Why does oogenesis involve an unequal division of cytoplasm?

options.A: To make sure polar bodies grow into backup eggs
options.B: To speed up the final stages of cell division
options.C: To provide the fertilized egg with enough stored food and nutrients
options.D: To balance the exact number of X and Y chromosomes

explanation: By packing most of the cytoplasm into one egg cell, the body ensures the early embryo has enough energy to survive its first few days. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h2)

question: Where does sperm production take place in the male body?
explanation: Sperm are produced inside the tiny, coiled tubes called seminiferous tubules located within the testes. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h3)

question: How is spermatogenesis different from oogenesis in its final outcome?

options.A: Spermatogenesis produces four equal-sized functional sperm cells
options.B: Spermatogenesis creates polar bodies that absorb nutrients
options.C: Spermatogenesis stops completely in middle age

explanation: While female cell division makes one large egg and tiny polar bodies, male cell division splits the cytoplasm evenly to make four working sperm. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT true about normal oogenesis?

options.A: Cells pause in development for many years
options.B: Continuous daily production of thousands of new eggs throughout life
options.C: Final division finishes only after fertilization
options.D: Unequal division of cytoplasm creates polar bodies

explanation: Unlike men who make sperm every day, women are born with a set number of eggs that gradually decrease over time. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why is a sperm cell built so differently from an egg cell?

options.A: Eggs need tails to swim toward the sperm
options.B: Sperm need large amounts of cytoplasm to survive
options.C: Sperm contain multiple nuclei for cell fusion
options.D: Sperm are built for swimming, while eggs store nutrients for growth

explanation: A sperm sheds most of its cytoplasm to stay light and fast for travel, while an egg keeps its cytoplasm to feed the early embryo. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why is the risk of chromosomal issues higher for older pregnant women?

options.A: Her eggs have been paused in development for decades and can fail to separate properly
options.B: Her ovaries make new germ cells rapidly
options.C: Her uterine lining lacks hormones for cell division
options.D: Her body produces excess polar bodies

explanation: Because a woman's eggs stay paused in early meiosis for many years, the cellular equipment can sometimes struggle to separate chromosomes correctly as she ages. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h5)

question: How does ongoing sperm production relate to genetic changes over time?

options.A: Frequent cell division in older men can lead to copied mistakes or mutations
options.B: Spermatogenesis stops at age forty to prevent errors
options.C: Sperm cells are immune to genetic aging because they renew daily
options.D: Male cells pause in meiosis and cause high rates of Down syndrome

explanation: Because sperm-producing cells keep dividing throughout a man's life, the DNA is copied repeatedly, which can occasionally introduce small spelling mistakes over time. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T1#BMP210_U4_T1_h5)

question: Where does fertilization of the egg normally happen in the body?
explanation: The ampulla is the widest part of the fallopian tube where the sperm and egg usually meet. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why do so many sperm fail to reach the egg on their journey through the female reproductive tract?

options.A: Rapid absorption into the uterine wall lining
options.B: Hostile acidic vaginal environment and physical barriers
options.C: Immediate destruction by the ovary before entering the tube
options.D: Lack of seminal fluid to propel them past the cervix

explanation: The vagina is naturally acidic, and thick mucus at the cervix traps or stops most sperm before they make it to the tubes. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of sperm capacitation inside the female reproductive tract?

options.A: To enable the sperm to fertilize the oocyte
options.B: To protect the sperm from immediate vaginal acidity
options.C: To guide the sperm directly into the ovary
options.D: To help the sperm multiply in number before reaching the egg

explanation: Capacitation changes the sperm membrane and movement so it gains the strength and ability to fertilize an egg. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h2)

question: A patient asks how long sperm can survive and wait for ovulation in the female tract. What is the best response?
explanation: Capacitated sperm can live in the female tract for up to five days, which is why intercourse a few days before ovulation can still result in pregnancy. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which enzyme is released by the sperm to help it digest a path through the outer layer of the egg?
explanation: Acrosin is a specialized enzyme stored in the sperm head that breaks down the protective outer layer of the egg. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h3)

question: What triggers a sperm cell to start releasing its digestive enzymes?

options.A: Physical friction against the walls of the fallopian tube
options.B: Exposure to the alkaline fluid inside the uterine cavity
options.C: Chemical signals released directly from the mature ovary
options.D: Contact with the specific proteins of the zona pellucida

explanation: Touching the outer layer of the egg causes the sperm to release its enzymes so it can break through. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h3)

question: What exact event happens right after the sperm successfully breaks through the outer shell of the egg?

options.A: Disintegration of the remaining corona radiata
options.B: Cleavage of the zygote into four distinct cells
options.C: Fusion of the sperm and oocyte plasma membranes
options.D: Immediate breakdown of the entire uterine lining

explanation: Once through the outer layer, the outer membrane of the sperm touches and fuses with the membrane of the egg. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which cellular event is triggered inside the egg the moment a sperm enters its cytoplasm?

options.A: Reversal of the first mitotic cell division
options.B: Immediate replication of maternal DNA strands
options.C: Destruction of the cell nucleus to form a blastocyst
options.D: Completion of the second meiotic division

explanation: Sperm entry acts as a signal for the egg to finish its final cell division process. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is the main danger if more than one sperm fertilizes an egg?

options.A: Premature shedding of the uterine decidua
options.B: An abnormal and fatal number of chromosomes
options.C: Immediate implantation outside the uterine cavity
options.D: Complete failure of the placenta to develop

explanation: If multiple sperm enter the egg, it introduces too many chromosomes, which prevents normal human development. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which cellular change helps prevent more than one sperm from entering the egg?

options.A: Complete cessation of maternal heartbeat and circulation
options.B: Rapid dissolution of the entire secondary oocyte membrane
options.C: Hardening and modification of the zona pellucida by cortical granule enzymes
options.D: Instantaneous shedding of all remaining follicular cells

explanation: Enzymes from the egg quickly change the outer shell so extra sperm can no longer attach or enter. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is formed the exact moment the male and female genetic material combine?
explanation: The single cell formed when the male and female genetic materials join together is called a zygote. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h6)

question: Why is restoring the normal chromosome count during fertilization important for the baby?

options.A: It ensures the baby receives the correct total of forty-six chromosomes
options.B: It stops the mother from experiencing early pregnancy symptoms
options.C: It prevents the placenta from attaching too deeply into the uterus
options.D: It guarantees that the baby will develop into a male child

explanation: Combining 23 chromosomes from the sperm and 23 from the egg gives the baby the normal total of 46 needed for healthy growth. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T2#BMP210_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the very first cell called immediately after fertilization occurs?
explanation: The single cell formed right after the sperm and egg fuse together is known as the zygote. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why does the early embryo not increase in overall physical size during its initial divisions in the fallopian tube?

options.A: The mother's blood supply prevents it from absorbing nutrients.
options.B: Gravity pulls the cells together tightly to stop their growth.
options.C: Cells divide so fast they consume all available maternal oxygen.
options.D: It is contained within a rigid protective shell called the zona pellucida.

explanation: The zona pellucida acts like a boundary wrapper, keeping the total volume of the early dividing cells constant until it hatches later. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h1)

question: What are the individual cells called that form when the zygote splits during early cleavage?
explanation: As the zygote divides, each new smaller cell produced is called a blastomere. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h2)

question: What happens to the size of individual cells as the zygote goes through multiple rapid cleavage divisions?

options.A: They stay the exact same size while the zona pellucida expands.
options.B: They get smaller with each division because total volume stays fixed.
options.C: They grow larger by absorbing fluids from the fallopian tube.
options.D: They alternate between growing and shrinking randomly.

explanation: Because the zona pellucida confines the embryo, the cells divide without growing, resulting in smaller individual blastomeres. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h2)

question: At approximately how many cells does the embryo look like a mulberry and earn the name morula?
explanation: The morula stage is reached around the 16 to 32 cell mark, roughly four days after fertilization. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following describes compaction during early embryonic development?

options.A: Blastomeres flatten against each other and form tight junctions.
options.B: Fluid fills the center of the cell mass to form a cavity.
options.C: Sperm cells merge with the outer layer of the zygote.
options.D: The embryo breaks free from the fallopian tube wall.

explanation: Compaction is the process where loose cells pull tightly together to establish distinct inner and outer cellular compartments. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the fluid-filled cavity inside a developing blastocyst called?
explanation: The fluid-filled space that forms inside the blastocyst is the blastocoele or blastocystic cavity. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h4)

question: A student looks at a microscope slide of a 5-day-old human embryo and sees an outer layer of cells and an inner cell cluster. What primary structure are they looking at?
explanation: The presence of an inner cell mass and an outer trophoblast layer surrounding a fluid cavity defines the blastocyst stage. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h4)

question: What must the blastocyst do to its outer protective shell before it can attach to the uterine wall?

options.A: Absorb it completely into the ICM

explanation: The blastocyst must undergo hatching, breaking through the zona pellucida to expose its surface cells for implantation. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for preparing the uterine lining for successful blastocyst implantation?
explanation: Progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum transforms the endometrium into a thick, nutrient-rich secretory lining ready for pregnancy. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T3#BMP210_U4_T3_h5)

question: During a standard 28-day menstrual cycle, when does the window of implantation typically happen?
explanation: The uterine lining is most ready for a fertilized egg during the mid-luteal phase, which is days 20 to 24 of a normal cycle. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why is the timing of when the blastocyst arrives in the uterus so important?

options.A: Late arrival causes the ovaries to stop producing all estrogen.
options.B: Early arrival triggers an immediate immune rejection by the cervix.
options.C: The embryo runs out of stored nutrients if it floats too long.
options.D: The uterine lining is only receptive during a brief hormonal window.

explanation: Hormones control when the uterine lining is open to implantation, and this window stays open for only a short time. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h1)

question: What is the correct order of the three main phases of human implantation?
explanation: The process starts with loose contact (apposition), moves to secure attachment (adhesion), and finishes with tissue penetration (invasion). [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h2)

question: How does adhesion differ from apposition in early implantation?

options.A: Adhesion is mediated by red blood cells, whereas apposition uses white blood cells.
options.B: Adhesion involves firm molecular bonds, whereas apposition is loose physical contact.
options.C: Adhesion destroys maternal tissue directly, while apposition creates the placenta.
options.D: Adhesion occurs before ovulation, while apposition happens during menstruation.

explanation: Apposition simply brings the blastocyst close to the lining, while adhesion uses specific molecules to hold it firmly in place. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which layer of the trophoblast produces enzymes to break down maternal tissue during implantation?
explanation: The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer layer that releases special enzymes to help the embryo burrow into the uterine lining. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h3)

question: What is the main job of the cytotrophoblast during the invasion phase?

options.A: It acts as a physical barrier to prevent any maternal blood from entering.
options.B: It forms the umbilical cord vessels before embryonic circulation starts.
options.C: It produces large amounts of progesterone to maintain the corpus luteum.
options.D: It continuously divides to feed cells into the growing syncytiotrophoblast layer.

explanation: The cytotrophoblast acts as a cell factory, constantly dividing to supply new cells to the outer syncytiotrophoblast layer. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for the changes of the decidual reaction in the endometrium?
explanation: Progesterone prepares the uterine lining and triggers the cellular changes known as the decidual reaction. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is a key protective function of the decidual reaction when the embryo implants?

options.A: It completely stops all maternal blood flow to the uterus to prevent bleeding.
options.B: It accelerates the heartbeat of the embryo before the heart is fully formed.
options.C: It controls and limits how deeply the trophoblast can invade the uterine wall.
options.D: It transforms the blastocyst into a multi-layered amniotic cavity.

explanation: Decidualization acts like a brake system, stopping the embryo from burrowing too deep into the muscular uterine wall. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which part of the decidua lies directly underneath the implanted blastocyst and helps form the placenta?
explanation: The decidua basalis is located right at the base of the conceptus and plays a direct role in building the maternal side of the placenta. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h5)

question: What happens to the decidua capsularis as the fetus and amniotic sac grow during pregnancy?

options.A: It thickens into a muscular wall that takes over the function of the myometrium.
options.B: It stretches, thins out, and eventually fuses with the decidua parietalis.
options.C: It transforms directly into the umbilical cord to supply oxygen to the fetus.
options.D: It detaches from the uterus and is expelled through the cervix every trimester.

explanation: As the pregnancy sac expands, the decidua capsularis gets pushed outward until it merges with the opposite uterine wall. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h5)

question: What do we call it when a blastocyst implants outside the main uterine cavity, such as in the fallopian tube?
explanation: Any pregnancy that implants outside the uterus is called an ectopic pregnancy, with the fallopian tubes being the most common spot. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h6)

question: A pregnant patient with past uterine surgeries has trouble with the placenta failing to separate after birth. What is the most likely condition?
explanation: Previous uterine scars can disrupt normal decidua formation, causing the placenta to attach abnormally deep into the muscle wall. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T4#BMP210_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the solid ball of about 16 cells formed during early cleavage called?
explanation: The early embryo reaches a 16-cell solid clump that looks like a tiny mulberry, which is called a morula before it develops an inner cavity. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T5#BMP210_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why does the early embryo divide rapidly without getting bigger in overall size?

options.A: To speed up the production of amniotic fluid inside the uterus
options.B: To allow the yolk sac to form properly before implantation
options.C: To prevent the mother's immune system from attacking the cells
options.D: To fit through the narrow Fallopian tube while dividing its cells

explanation: The outer shell keeps the dividing cells contained to the original size of the zygote so the tiny mass can travel safely down the narrow Fallopian tube. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T5#BMP210_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which primary germ layer gives rise to the nervous system and skin?
explanation: The ectoderm is the outer germ layer that develops into structures interacting with the outside world, such as the nervous system and the outer layer of skin. [learn more](BMP210_U4_T5#BMP210_U4_T5_h2)

question: During which timeframe is a developing baby most vulnerable to structural birth defects from harmful substances?
